claims.text: Most offices today feature an open design plan.
claims.argument: SHRM cites experts saying roughly 70 percent of offices have some sort of open floor plan. A CommercialCafé article cites Gallup for nearly 70% of U.S. offices using an open plan. A Bloomberg-attributed 75% figure appears in secondary sources. These look like one repeated, older estimate, and "some sort of open plan" is loose wording. No source contradicts "most", so the claim is plausible, though no current authoritative statistic was found.
claims.summary: No current, authoritative national figure confirms the share of offices with open plans.

claims.text: Open office design is great for collaboration and cutting costs, but most employees are less productive because of it.
claims.argument: A 2018 Harvard Business School field study found face-to-face interaction fell by about 69-72% after moves to open offices, with email use rising. That contradicts the claim that open offices are "great for collaboration". The productivity decline in that study came from executives' reports at one firm, not from measurements. The largest survey (Kim & de Dear, 2013) found that many workers in open-plan offices were unhappy with sound privacy. Satisfaction is linked to perceived productivity, but no source shows that most employees are measurably less productive. The cost-saving point is conventional and was not disputed.
claims.summary: Open offices often cut costs, but they reduced face-to-face talk, and proof that most workers are less productive is thin.

claims.text: Employees are less productive in open offices because they are dissatisfied with their work environment.
claims.argument: Research does show open-plan offices bring more dissatisfaction, especially about sound privacy (a University of Sydney study of 303 buildings). Evidence of actual productivity loss is mixed: a Leesman review of 84,158 employees found open plans do not all harm productivity, and most findings rely on self-reported perception. The Bernstein and Turban study found about 70% less face-to-face interaction after moves to open offices, and executives at one company reported lower performance metrics, but that is not a general causal finding. The claim that dissatisfaction is the cause of lower productivity is the speaker's own explanation and is not established.
claims.summary: Open offices often cause noise complaints and dissatisfaction, but proof of lower productivity, and that dissatisfaction causes it, is weaker.

claims.text: A lack of sound and visual privacy is by far and away the biggest drain on employee morale.
claims.argument: The claim echoes the 2013 University of Sydney study by Kim and de Dear, which used about 43,000 survey responses from 303 buildings. It found open-plan workers were most dissatisfied with sound privacy (roughly 50-60% unhappy), and 20-40% were unhappy with visual privacy. Trade press such as HR Reporter described sound privacy as the biggest drain on morale. "By far and away" and "morale" are looser than the study's wording on dissatisfaction, but the substance is supported.
claims.summary: Not applicable.

claims.text: Cubicall booths focus on four pillars of privacy needs: audio, visual, territorial, and information.
claims.argument: Acoustic, visual, territorial and informational privacy are an established way to describe workplace privacy; Steelcase and Penketh Group both list these four. No retrieved Cubicall page mentions "four pillars" or this framework. Its product page describes the Two Series phone booth and Four Series meeting room only in general terms. The claim is the company's own marketing wording, so the sources neither confirm nor contradict it.
claims.summary: The four privacy types are real, but no source shows Cubicall uses them as its "pillars".

claims.text: Cubicall booths are fully customizable, available in a variety of colors, materials and custom graphics, and have bifolding doors that let them fit into offices where space is critical.
claims.argument: Cubicall's own listings describe its booths as customizable, with walls that can have almost any color, finish or custom printed graphics. A 2017 press release confirms custom graphics, such as classic artwork. Its patented designs use space-saving bi-fold doors that help them fit tight spaces and meet building codes. No itemized list of materials was found, but the "finish" options support the claim.
claims.summary: Cubicall booths can be customized with colors and graphics, and they use space-saving bi-fold doors.

claims.text: Cubicall booths come with an air circulation fan and a regular outlet so a laptop and two USB chargers can be plugged in.
claims.argument: Cubicall's official Two Series page lists dual-fan air circulation (up to 108 cfm), 120-volt outlets and USB-A/USB-C ports. The 2021 catalog also describes the fan and a 120v outlet. The speaker's "air circulation fan" and "regular outlet" for a laptop and USB chargers match these specs. The exact number of outlets and USB ports varies by model and year, so the pitch is a loose summary of the spec, not a verbatim one.
claims.summary: Exact outlet and USB counts per booth could not be confirmed.

claims.text: The Cubicall 2 booth sells for $6,995.
claims.argument: A Workdesign marketplace listing gives Cubicall privacy pods a starting price of $6,995 and describes the Two Series as the company's original phone booth. That fits the speaker's "$6,995" for the Cubicall 2. Other sources give different figures: older Shark Tank coverage lists $6,495 to $11,995, and some sites cite $7,995 for a newer or single-person booth. These differ by date or model and do not contradict a $6,995 price in the 2026 pitch. The $11,995 price for the larger booth is also consistent with the older coverage.
claims.summary: Only one listing gives $6,995, and it does not clearly tie the price to the Cubicall 2.

claims.text: The Cubicall 2 booth costs $4,200 to make.
claims.argument: Recaps of the Shark Tank pitch say the smaller Cubicall booth sold for about $7,000 and cost $4,200 to make. The larger booth sold for about $12,000 and cost $7,200 to make. That matches the speaker's figures ($4,200 and $7,200). The figure is the founders' own pitch claim, not independently audited. The only sources found that give it are low-quality aggregator sites, so the verdict rests on thin evidence.
claims.summary: The $4,200 cost comes from the founders' own pitch and low-quality recap pages, with no company confirmation.

claims.text: The bigger Cubicall booth sells for $11,995.
claims.argument: The Shark Tank Blog lists Cubicall booths as ranging from $6,495 to $11,995, so $11,995 is the top price. A separate listing gives $6,995 as the starting price, which matches the smaller booth the speaker quotes. One article suggests prices have since risen, but that is unverified against the company's own site. The speaker's "$11,9.95" is a transcription of $11,995.
claims.summary: Current 2026 Cubicall pricing for the largest booth could not be checked on the company's own site.

claims.text: The bigger Cubicall booth costs $7,200 to make.
claims.argument: In the pitch, the founder says the larger booth sells for $11,995 and costs $7,200 to make. A secondary article on the Shark Tank pitch gives the same figures: about $12,000 sale price, $7,200 cost, and $4,200 cost for the smaller booth at about $7,000. Shark Tank Blog's price range tops out at $11,995, which fits. The cost is the founder's own statement; no independent source or company filing was found to verify it.
claims.summary: The $7,200 cost comes only from the founder's pitch and one weak write-up, with no independent check.

claims.text: Competitors sell comparable booths for about $15,000.
claims.argument: Competitor prices are a wide range. Zenbooth runs from about $4,495 to $15,995 for the largest model. Framery's single-person booth is listed at roughly $8,000-$13,000, and ROOM's at about $5,000-$6,500. The $15,000 figure fits larger multi-person booths against Cubicall's $11,995 big unit. It does not fit smaller booths against the $6,995 unit. As a rough, pitch-style claim it is partly supported but overstated as a general competitor price.
claims.summary: Some large competitor booths cost about $15,000, but many comparable booths cost much less.

claims.text: The Cubicall founders started their own marketing agency in an open plan office, and it is a family business.
claims.argument: Reports say Cubicall was founded by brothers Nick and Anthony Pucci, long-time marketing executives. The idea came from noisy calls in their own open-plan marketing agency, where they had to leave the office to take calls. The "family business" detail is simply the brothers working together, and it comes from their own account on the show. No source contradicts it.
claims.summary: The brothers did start a marketing agency in an open office; the family-business part is their own statement.

claims.text: Cubicall has sold about 70 booths.
claims.argument: The claim reports what the founder said on Shark Tank (Season 10, 2019): about 70 booths sold. Shark Tank Blog reports about $500,000 in sales over a year. That matches the $495,000 figure the founder stated. One lower-quality site also cites seventy units. The unit count is not independently verified beyond the pitch itself.
claims.summary: The 70-booth count appears only in the founder's pitch and one weak site.

claims.text: Cubicall's sales over the last 12 months were $495,000.
claims.argument: Write-ups of the Cubicall Shark Tank pitch (about 70 booths sold, asking $350,000 for 10%) report roughly $500,000 in sales over the prior 12 months. One site gives the exact figure of $495,000 from seventy units, which matches the claim. The figure is the founder's own statement on the show, not independently audited, and the sources that give it are secondary, some of low quality.
claims.summary: Only a weak site gives the exact $495,000 figure; other write-ups say about $500,000.

claims.text: Cubicall started the business last August.
claims.argument: The words are from a Shark Tank Season 10 pitch (aired May 2019), so "last August" refers to the time of filming, not to 2026. Sources say the Pucci brothers founded Cubicall in 2017, which fits an August 2017 start if the pitch was filmed in 2018. No retrieved source confirms the exact month, and the sources do not contradict it. The claim is plausible as a report of what the founder said, but the August date is unverified.
claims.summary: No source gives the exact month Cubicall started, so "August" is not confirmed.

claims.text: Cubicall makes $1,800 on the 6K version of its booth.
claims.argument: The searches found Shark Tank coverage of Cubicall, but nothing giving a per-booth profit on a "6K" model. Prices reported range from about $6,495 to $11,995, so a roughly $6,000 entry booth is plausible. One low-quality site implies a different margin, about $2,800 on a $7,000 booth, but it gives no source. The $1,800 figure appears to come from a Shark's remark in the episode, and no source checks it.
claims.summary: No reliable source confirms the $1,800 profit on the $6K booth.

claims.text: Cubicall's margins are so thin that the only way the business works is selling direct to customers.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: If Cubicall gets the investment to invest in inventory, it will be able to widen its margins by another 20 to 30%.
claims.argument: No fact check available — this is a prediction about the future, which no source can confirm yet.

claims.text: Cubicall wants to reach $2.5 million in sales next year, which is about 300 booths.
claims.argument: No fact check available — this is a prediction about the future, which no source can confirm yet.

claims.text: In the whole market there are probably about four competitors that Cubicall competes with.
claims.argument: The founder's "about four competitors" is a rough, subjective estimate, so no source can confirm or refute the exact count. CB Insights lists TalkBox, Framery, Orosound, H4D, Poppin and about seven more as competitors. A business journal piece also names Zenbooth and notes that Chinese makers are entering the market. The estimate could be defensible if it means only close rivals with similar mid-priced booths, but the wider market is clearly bigger than four.
claims.summary: The founder said about four rivals, but the market has many more office phone booth makers.

claims.text: Nobody else makes a bifold door for office booths.
claims.argument: Shark Tank fan sites repeat Cubicall's line that none of its roughly four competitors makes a bifold door; these are promotional-leaning sources. A TalkBox press release describes a booth with a "folding door designed for ease of use and soundproofing," which may be a bifold-type door. The release does not say the door is a true bifold. Other booths use sliding or hinged doors. The claim is plausible as a marketing claim, but "nobody else" is too absolute and is not independently verified.
claims.summary: Cubicall's bifold door is unusual, but a rival, TalkBox, has sold a booth with a folding door.

claims.text: 80% of all offices are open plan offices.
claims.argument: An 80% figure appears in secondary summaries, attributed to Sage research. Other secondary sources give about 70% (Forbes-cited), 75% (Bloomberg-cited), and as low as 15-20% (Fortune-cited) or 23% globally (AIA-cited). Definitions of "open plan" vary, and no primary study was found. The speaker also hedged with "they do say". The figure is a commonly cited but unverified estimate.
claims.summary: The 80% figure is repeated online, but estimates range from about 15% to 80% and none has a solid source.

claims.text: There are by estimates maybe about 9.1 million businesses in the US.
claims.argument: The figure of roughly 9 million matches commercial estimates of US establishments with employees (IBISWorld puts it near 9 million, with an 8.6 million estimate for 2025). However, Census data show about 5.9 million employer firms (2023) and roughly 30 million nonemployer businesses (29.8 million in 2022, 32 million in 2024). Whether "9.1 million businesses" is right depends on the definition. It is a loose, hedged figure that leaves out most US businesses, and no source gives exactly 9.1 million.
claims.summary: About 9 million fits only businesses with employees; counting one-person businesses, the US has over 35 million.

claims.text: When a company's own sales projection relies on capturing one-tenth of 1% of a big market, it is a kiss of death on Shark Tank.
claims.argument: The line is a Shark's opinion in the Cubicall pitch (Season 10), where the founders asked $350,000 for 10% and Barbara Corcoran countered at 25%. Mark Cuban is reported to warn against pitches like "it's a $7.3 billion market and I just need 1%", which draws immediate skepticism. That supports the general idea. "Kiss of death" is a figure of speech, not a measured rule. The retrieved sources did not include the episode transcript or an authoritative source, and Cubicall still got a deal despite the pitch.
claims.summary: No transcript was found that confirms how the Shark worded the "kiss of death" remark.

claims.text: Kevin offered $350,000 for 10% of the company, plus $100 for every unit sold until he recovers $1,050,000 (three times his original investment), after which it drops to $50 a unit forever.
claims.argument: The video's transcript has Kevin offering $350,000 for 10% and $100 per unit sold. The royalty drops to $50 a unit "forever" after he recovers three times his investment. The transcript garbles the figure as "1,50,000", but three times $350,000 is $1,050,000, so the claim's number is consistent. Written sources confirm O'Leary offered $350,000 for 10% with a $100-per-unit royalty. None of the retrieved sources mention the $50 step-down. Barbara later countered, and the Cubicall deal was reportedly with her.
claims.summary: Kevin offered $350,000 for 10% plus $100 a unit; $1,050,000 is three times $350,000.

claims.text: Barbara offered $350,000 for 25% of the Cubicall business.
claims.argument: Recaps of the Cubicall Shark Tank pitch say the Pucci brothers asked $350,000 for 10%. Kevin O'Leary offered the same amount with a royalty. Barbara Corcoran offered $350,000 for 25% with no royalties, and the founders took her deal. This matches the quoted line "350,000 for 25% of the business". The sources are secondary recaps, not the episode itself.
claims.summary: Barbara offered $350,000 for 25% of Cubicall, as the speaker says, and the founders accepted.

claims.text: When a company is sold, a royalty holder's royalty is bought out by the acquirer, which has happened to many of Kevin's companies.
claims.argument: Royalty buyouts at a sale are a common deal feature, and royalty clauses often say what happens on a sale. No retrieved source documents Kevin O'Leary's royalties being bought out by acquirers in "many" of his companies. A fan blog mentions only one royalty buyout, Wicked Good Cupcakes, and there the founders bought it out, not an acquirer. The claim is Kevin's own statement in the show, and it neither checks out nor is contradicted by the sources found.
claims.summary: No reliable source confirms that buyers bought out Kevin's royalties in many of his companies.

claims.text: Anthony and Nick Poochie countered Barbara with $350,000 for 15% of the company, and Barbara turned it down.
claims.argument: The speaker's own transcript has the founders saying "we would like to counter with 350 for 15%" and Barbara replying "It's not enough... I'd have to turn that down." Recaps agree that Barbara's offer was $350,000 for 25% and that the founders (the Pucci brothers, Nick and Anthony; "Poochie" is a mis-transcription) eventually took her 25% deal. This matches a 15% counter that she rejected first. No recap states the 15% counter explicitly, and the quality of the sources is mixed.
claims.summary: The brothers countered Barbara with $350,000 for 15% and she said no; their name is Pucci.

claims.text: Barbara claims to have tremendous contacts in the contract furniture space and says she can make the right introductions for Cubicall.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: Anthony and Nick Poochie then proposed $450,000 for 20% of the company, and Barbara refused, saying she needs the 25% slice to get excited about it.
claims.argument: Write-ups of the Cubicall pitch (Season 10, 2019) say Barbara Corcoran offered $350,000 for 25%. The Puccis countered with 15%. She said she could only get excited about 25%, and they eventually accepted. The episode dialogue quoted in the context has "How about can we do 450 for 20?" followed by "No... I need that quarter slice to get really juiced up about it," which matches the claim. "Poochie" is a transcription slip for Pucci. The summaries retrieved do not mention the $450K/20% counter, so that detail rests on the episode dialogue alone.
claims.summary: No outside source confirms the $450,000-for-20% counteroffer, only the episode's own dialogue.

claims.text: The Cubicall founders Anthony and Nick Poochie accepted Barbara's deal after she refused to budge on the equity, after their counteroffer of 450 for 20% was rejected.
claims.argument: Reports on the Season 10 Cubicall pitch say Barbara Corcoran offered $350,000 for 25%, the founders pushed back, she held at 25%, and they accepted. This matches the claim that she would not budge on equity and they took the deal. The founders' surname is Pucci, so "Poochie" is most likely a transcription slip. The specific "450 for 20%" counteroffer was not found in the written recaps, though it is plausible as a step in the on-air back-and-forth. The recaps give different figures for the earlier negotiation steps, which leaves some doubt on that detail.
claims.summary: The exact 450-for-20% counteroffer could not be checked in written sources.

claims.text: Shane Penel is seeking a $40,000 investment for 25% equity in his company, Sweep Easy.
claims.argument: Multiple sources on the Shark Tank Season 2, Episode 6 pitch say Shane Pannell sought $40,000 for a 25% stake in Sweep Easy. The ask matches the claim. The name is spelled Pannell in the sources rather than "Penel", which is a transcription variant.
claims.summary: He did ask for $40,000 for 25% of Sweep Easy; his surname is spelled Pannell.

claims.text: For centuries the common house broom has been used as a tool to help people clean their floors.
claims.argument: Brooms made of bundled twigs or plant fibers have been used for sweeping since ancient times. Besoms were used in Anglo-Saxon and Tudor England to sweep dirt, stone and brick floors. The flat broom was developed by the Shakers around 1797-1798. "For centuries" is accurate for a household broom used to clean floors.
claims.summary: Brooms have been used to sweep floors for many centuries, as he says.

claims.text: Shane Penel's Sweep Easy Scrape and Go Broom has a patent pending.
claims.argument: Coverage of the Shark Tank pitch (Season 2, 2011) says Shane Pannell's patent was still pending and that he had not yet sold any brooms. This matches the quote in the video. The name is spelled Pannell in most sources, not "Penel", which is a minor spelling difference. The pitch dates from 2011 and was uploaded in 2026, and the claim holds as of the pitch. A later patent, US10349735 for a scrape-and-sweep broom handle attachment, may be linked to the product, but that link was not confirmed. No USPTO filing record was opened to check the pending status directly.
claims.summary: No patent filing record was opened to confirm the pending status directly.

claims.text: Shane Penel has not sold any Sweep Easy brooms yet because he is working with prototypes that he made himself.
claims.argument: The claim matches what the inventor, spelled Shane Pannell in sources, said in his Shark Tank pitch. Summaries of the episode say his patent was pending, he hadn't yet sold any brooms, and he had prototypes. Local coverage years later says he finally got the product to market. That fits the claim, which describes the time of the pitch. The speaker's name is spelled "Penel" in the transcript, which is only a spelling variation.
claims.summary: At his Shark Tank pitch, Shane said he hadn't sold any brooms yet because he only had self-made prototypes.

claims.text: Robert said he is the only one among the Sharks who has actually swept the floor, because he was a stay-at-home dad for 3 years.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: Shane Penel said in the pitch that the company that asked when he could have a finished product had not yet given him a purchase order for Sweep Easy.
claims.argument: The name is Shane Panell (also spelled Pannell), whose Sweep Easy was pitched on Shark Tank season 2, episode 205. A recap says he had no purchase orders yet, which fits the rendering. No transcript with the janitorial-company exchange or the "licensed, bonded, insured" reason was retrieved, so the exact wording is unverified.
claims.summary: The exact on-air words could not be found, though the pitch is real.

quote.author: Shane Penel
quote.quoted_text: They didn't give me a purchase order yet

claims.text: If the Sweep Easy broom could be sold direct to the consumer, you could build a $100 million business on a single product.
claims.argument: No fact check available — this is a prediction about the future, which no source can confirm yet.

claims.text: Shane Penel said that he canvassed restaurants, movie theaters, hospitals and schools, asked what they would pay for something like Sweep Easy, and that the answer was always the same: 1995.
claims.argument: Articles confirm that Shane Pannell (spelled "Penel" in the captions) pitched SweepEasy on Shark Tank Season 2, Episode 6. No transcript or article carrying the restaurants, theaters, hospitals and schools remark was found. "1995" is most likely a caption rendering of "$19.95", though this is unconfirmed.
claims.summary: The exact words could not be found in any written source.

quote.author: Shane Penel
quote.quoted_text: I'd beat the pavement and restaurants, movie theaters, hospitals, schools, everywhere I've gone and I ask them, "What would you pay for something like this?" And the answer is always the same. 1995.

claims.text: A shark offered $40,000 for 20% of the company, then another offered $50,000 for 20%.
claims.argument: Recaps of the Sweep Easy pitch (Shark Tank season 2) describe an opening offer of $40,000 for 20%, followed by a raised offer of $50,000 for 20%. Recaps differ on which shark made the second offer: one says O'Leary raised his own bid, and the video's wording suggests a different shark. The claim says only "another", so this does not change its core. The final deal was reportedly different ($80,000 for 25%) and never closed.
claims.summary: Sources disagree on which shark made the second offer.

claims.text: Licensing a product yields about 30 to 40% of the income that can be made on it at the end of the day.
claims.argument: A Shark Tank recap confirms that Kevin Harrington made this remark about Sweep Easy, saying licensing brings roughly 30-40% of what direct sales would earn. That only shows what he said; it is not an independent check. General licensing sources put royalties at about 3-15% of net sales, but they do not compare that with what selling the product yourself earns. The figure is therefore an opinion about this product that neither a source nor the general data confirms or refutes.
claims.summary: The 30–40% figure is one Shark's opinion on the show; no source confirms it as a general rule.

claims.text: A shark on Shark Tank offered $50,000 for 20% of Sweep Easy under a licensing strategy.
claims.argument: Summaries of the episode say Kevin O'Leary pushed licensing and first offered $40,000 for 20%. He then raised it to $50,000 for 20% if the entrepreneur would "stop listening to these guys". That matches the speaker's quote. The claim does not say the offer was accepted, and the final deal on air was a different one.
claims.summary: Kevin O'Leary did offer $50,000 for 20% of Sweep Easy, pushing a licensing plan.

claims.text: Mr. Wonderful says that Fubu, which he created in a basement, branded a pair of jeans globally, and that he will do the same with the broom.
claims.argument: Fubu was founded by Daymond John, who started it in his parents' home in Queens. Kevin O'Leary (Mr. Wonderful) did not create Fubu. The speaker's own context ("Whether you like Fubu or not, I created...") fits Daymond John, who also bid on Sweep Easy. No episode transcript was retrieved to show the exact line, so this rests on who founded Fubu.
claims.summary: Fubu is Daymond John's company, so these words most likely came from him, not Mr. Wonderful.

quote.author: Mr. Wonderful
quote.quoted_text: I created in the basement and everybody on the story planet knows.

claims.text: David offered $75,000 for 33% of the company.
claims.argument: Summaries of the Sweep Easy episode (Season 2) quote Daymond John saying "I'm bringing $75,000 for 33%, but we'll create an entire company." This matches the claim's amount and stake. The "David" in the transcript is almost certainly a caption error for Daymond, as no Shark named David appears in that episode. The offer later changed to $80,000 for 25% with Kevin Harrington, but the $75,000 for 33% offer was made first.
claims.summary: Sources give the $75,000 for 33% offer but name Daymond John, not David.

claims.text: The founders originally came in asking for $40,000 for 25% of the company.
claims.argument: Several sources report that Sweep Easy's founder asked for $40,000 for 25% equity on Shark Tank Season 2. The ask matches the claim. The sources differ on the final deal terms, but that does not affect the ask. The claim says "founders" (plural), while the sources name one founder, Shane Pannell. This is a minor wording point.
claims.summary: The Sweep Easy inventor asked for $40,000 for 25%, as the speaker says.

claims.text: During the Shark Tank negotiation over Sweep Easy, one shark's combined offer rose to $80,000 for 25% of the company.
claims.argument: Recaps of the Sweep Easy pitch say Kevin O'Leary started at $40,000 for 20%. Robert Herjavec then joined him, making the offer $80,000, and it was raised to 25%. The transcript quoted in the claim matches this. Sources disagree on which sharks ended up with the final deal and on whether it closed, but that does not affect the claim that one shark's combined offer rose to $80,000 for 25%.
claims.summary: On the show, the offer did rise to $80,000 for 25%, as he says.

claims.text: Shane Penel, one of the sharks, lowered his offer from $40,000 to $30,000, making his deal $70,000, and later went in for the $80,000 deal with Damon, and the sharks closed a deal with the Sweep Easy founders.
claims.argument: Shane Pannell is the Sweep Easy founder who pitched in Season 2 (2011). He is not a shark. He asked for $40,000 for 25%, and Daymond John and Kevin Harrington offered $80,000, which he accepted on air. The speaker who cut $40,000 to $30,000 was a shark, so the claim misattributes the offer. Several sources say the deal was never finalized after filming, so "closed a deal" holds only for the on-air moment.
claims.summary: Shane Pannell is the inventor pitching, not a shark, and the on-air deal reportedly never actually closed.

claims.text: Jane Carol was born and raised in the Bronx, New York.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: Jane Carol is seeking $300,000 for 15% of her company, Jane Foodie.
claims.argument: Shark Tank trackers report that Jane Carroll (spelled "Carol" in the video) pitched Jane Foodie on Season 16 seeking $300,000 for 15% equity, a $2 million valuation. She ended up taking Lori Greiner's offer of $300,000 for 25%. The surname spelling differs between sources but does not affect the ask.
claims.summary: Not applicable.

claims.text: A Shark Tank pitcher in a clip said they found themselves wandering in the grocery store looking at the labels, thinking "Oh my god, what's in our food?", and that even the freezer section was loaded with preservatives.
claims.argument: Recaps confirm that Jane Carroll pitched Jane Foodie on Shark Tank Season 16 for $300,000 for 15%. They say the freezer is her "nature's preservative" and that she criticizes preservative-heavy store food. No transcript was found that prints her exact opening words, so the wording could not be checked. Nothing found contradicts the quote.
claims.summary: No transcript of the pitch was found, though recaps match the story of the pitch.

quote.author: Shark Tank pitcher in the clip (speaker in the inserted clip)
quote.quoted_text: I found myself wandering in the grocery store looking at the labels and thinking, "Oh my god, what's in our food?" Even the freezer section was loaded with preservatives.

claims.text: Flash freezing takes food directly from the oven down to -40 in 90 minutes.
claims.argument: Coverage of Jane Foodie says meals are flash-frozen at -40°F immediately after cooking, which matches the temperature part of the claim. No source found gives a 90-minute timeframe. General blast-freezing guidance suggests reaching a frozen core typically takes about 3–4 hours, though that is generic and not Jane Foodie's own process. The 90-minute figure is therefore a company pitch statement that could not be verified.
claims.summary: Jane Foodie freezes food right after cooking at -40, but no source confirms the 90-minute time.

claims.text: Flash freezing allows food to retain all of its flavors, textures, and nutrients.
claims.argument: Rapid freezing makes small ice crystals, which protects texture and nutrients better than slow freezing. America's Test Kitchen found 4% weight loss on thawing for very fast freezing, not zero. Nutrient losses are modest, typically under 10% for some vitamins, and some foods suffer more. "All" is therefore an overstatement. Sources are mostly trade and consumer pages, not primary studies.
claims.summary: Fast freezing keeps most flavor, texture and nutrients, but not literally all of them.

tags.name: About all, no exceptions
tags.subtype_name: 'always / never / all' as a literal claim
tags.definition: A statement about a whole class, or an 'always / never', is stronger than the data given.

evidence.text: This process allows the food to retain all of its flavors, textures, and nutrients.

tags.explanation: Sald as «retain all of its flavors, textures, and nutrients», an absolute with no qualifier.

claims.text: Flash freezing food is 40-year-old technology.
claims.argument: Clarence Birdseye pioneered commercial quick (flash) freezing in the 1920s: his company was formed in 1923 and his first freezer worked in 1924. His 1927 multiplate freezer patent was used for decades. The individually quick frozen (IQF) fluidized-bed freezer, a later refinement, dates to 1959-62, which is more than 60 years before 2026. Either way, the technology is far older than 40 years. The other speaker's reply that it is about 100 years old is closer to the record.
claims.summary: Flash freezing is about 100 years old, from the 1920s, not 40 years old.

claims.text: Frozen vegetables were flash frozen 100 years ago.
claims.argument: Clarence Birdseye developed quick-freezing in the 1920s (first process 1924; multiplate freezer patented 1927). Birds Eye frozen foods, including vegetables like spinach, went on sale in Springfield, Massachusetts, on March 6, 1930. Some sources call his patent the advent of flash freezing. The wording "flash frozen" is a modern term, and early vegetables needed blanching first, but the substance, that quick-frozen vegetables existed about 100 years ago, holds.
claims.summary: Sources do not say whether early vegetables were literally called flash frozen.

claims.text: Not all frozen food sold in stores is flash frozen.
claims.argument: Commercial freezing uses several methods: blast, plate, tunnel, fluidized-bed, cryogenic and IQF. Block-frozen items such as some meats are not individually quick frozen, and the freezing method is not required on labels. Sources conflict, though: one claims all commercial freezing is flash freezing. Quick freezing is very common for produce, so "not all" is accurate but the share that is not flash frozen is unclear.
claims.summary: Stores sell frozen foods made by different freezing methods, and not all are flash frozen.

claims.text: When food temperature is taken down very quickly, as in flash freezing, ice crystals don't form, so more vitamins and minerals are retained.
claims.argument: Fast freezing yields smaller ice crystals that damage cell walls less, but crystals still form, so "don't form" is an overstatement. Retention of vitamins and minerals is generally good in frozen produce, with the main losses coming from blanching and long storage. Sources found give no well-established vitamin gap between flash and slow freezing; the specific percentages come from low-quality sites. The claim is therefore directionally plausible but overstated.
claims.summary: Flash freezing makes smaller ice crystals, not none, and mainly protects texture; vitamin benefits are unproven.

claims.text: A Shark Tank pitcher in a clip, asked by the sharks to tell about themselves, said that years ago they created something called Boxed in Blooms, which was fresh flowers.
claims.argument: Jane Foodie's founder Jane Carroll appeared on Shark Tank Season 16. A Shark Tank blog says she earlier ran Boxed in Blooms, shipping fresh flowers. Other pages say it drew Oprah's attention and that she had a heart attack around 2008, which fits the clip. No transcript was retrieved, so the exact wording is not checked.
claims.summary: A blog confirms the Boxed in Blooms business, but no transcript of the pitch was found.

quote.author: Shark Tank pitcher in the clip (speaker in the inserted clip)
quote.quoted_text: Years ago, I created something called boxed in blooms. It was fresh flowers
quote.original_quote: She had another business in the past called Boxed in Blooms, shipping fresh flowers for sale.
quote.context: In the Shark Tank Season 16 pitch (aired 2025), Jane Foodie founder Jane Carroll told the sharks about her earlier business, Boxed in Blooms, which shipped fresh flowers. The video's clip matches this. The page found is a blog summary, not a transcript.

claims.text: Jane Carol's Boxed in Blooms ended up on Oprah's O list.
claims.argument: An artist profile for Jane Carroll says that in February 2002 her "Boxed In Blooms" was featured on Oprah's "O" List. A second site also says the arrangements caught Oprah's attention in 2002. Both sources are self-promotional or low-profile, and no Oprah or O Magazine archive was found to confirm it. The claim matches what these sources say, and nothing contradicts it.
claims.summary: Only a gallery bio and a Shark Tank fan site mention the Oprah feature; no Oprah source confirms it.

claims.text: In July 2008 Jane Foodie had a heart attack at the age of 41.
claims.argument: Jane Foodie's own site and Shark Tank sites say founder Jane Carroll had a heart attack at age 41 around 2008, during the financial crisis. These are mostly promotional or fan sources and are largely based on her own account. The heart attack, the age of 41 and the 2008 timing are consistent across them. No independent source for the exact month (July) was found, and none contradicts it.
claims.summary: The exact month, July 2008, is not confirmed by any independent source.

claims.text: In September 2008 the market crashed.
claims.argument: Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on September 15, 2008, and the Dow fell 504 points that day. On September 29, 2008 the Dow fell 777.68 points (6.98%), then the largest single-day point drop in its history. The market kept falling for weeks afterward, losing over 40% by November.
claims.summary: The stock market did crash in September 2008, with a record one-day Dow drop on September 29.

claims.text: Jane Foodie had a 99.9% blockage and ended up in the hospital.
claims.argument: "Jane Foodie" appears to be the stage name of Jane Carroll, founder of Jane Bakes. A CBS New York report says that within about 10 months her house burned down, she had a heart attack, and her flower business failed in the recession. A 2017 review dates the heart attack to July 2007, while the speaker says '08. The retrieved pages do not mention a 99.9% blockage or a hospital stay, so those details rest only on the speaker's own account.
claims.summary: A heart attack and failed flower business are reported, but the 99.9% blockage and hospital stay aren't confirmed.

claims.text: Jane Foodie's cardiologist told her she needed to start eating better.
claims.argument: This is a first-person anecdote: the speaker, apparently Jane Foodie, recounts what her cardiologist told her. Two searches found no interview, article or record of this exchange. A private doctor's remark like this is unlikely to be documented, so it can be neither confirmed nor refuted.
claims.summary: No record of the cardiologist's words was found; this is her own personal story.

quote.author: Jane Foodie's cardiologist
quote.quoted_text: Listen, you need to start eating better.

claims.text: Jane Foodie said she opened a little cafe and then got a phone call from a movie studio, which told her that her food is so healthy and asked whether she would be willing to come.
claims.argument: A profile of founder Jane Carroll says she had a heart attack at 41, opened a small coffeehouse, and then cooked for film crews, which led her to flash-freezing. That matches the broad story. No transcript of her own words was found, and the profile does not mention a phone call or the "your food is so healthy" line, so the quote itself cannot be verified.
claims.summary: The exact words were not found, though a profile matches the general story.

quote.author: Jane Foodie
quote.quoted_text: opened up a little cafe. And then I got a phone call from a movie studio and they said, "Listen, your food is so healthy. would you be willing to come

claims.text: Jane Foodie's company has sold a little over 1.1 million in sales to date.
claims.argument: Shark Tank recaps report that Jane Carroll told the Sharks she made $640,000 in 2023 and $580,000 so far in 2024, which adds up to just over $1.1 million. This matches what the speaker says she stated. The figure is her own pitch claim, repeated mostly by fan and aggregator sites. No audited or company-filed number was found to verify it independently. The speaker's "in one year" aside is a mistake by the host, since the figure covers two periods, but it is not part of the claim itself.
claims.summary: No company filing or audited record confirms the $1.1 million sales figure.

claims.text: In 2023 Jane Foodie's company did 640,000 in sales, and year to date it has done 580,000.
claims.argument: Shark Tank recap sites report that Jane Foodie made $640,000 in sales in 2023 and $580,000 so far in 2024, for a total of just over $1.1 million. This matches the figures the founder gave in her pitch. The "year to date" figure refers to the time of the pitch, which was filmed before the 2026 upload. The sources are secondary fan sites and no audited financials were found, so some doubt remains. They also describe the $1.1 million differently (lifetime versus annual), but the two figures in the claim are consistent.
claims.summary: Her pitch figures match Shark Tank recaps: $640,000 in 2023 and $580,000 so far in 2024.

claims.text: Jane Foodie's products are sold only in local stores, not in any major grocers, and she has no co-packer that flash freezes for her.
claims.argument: Coverage of the Shark Tank Season 16 pitch says Jane Foodie was in many local stores but not major grocery chains, and that Jane Carroll had no co-packer because she had not found one able to flash-freeze fresh food. This matches what the speaker says in the transcript. Sales were mostly local retail with about 10% online. A fan-run site claims later distribution in grocery stores across 27 states and on QVC, but that is unreliable and postdates the pitch. The claim is therefore accurate for the pitch-time situation it describes.
claims.summary: Whether she still has no co-packer or major grocer today is not confirmed by reliable sources.

claims.text: Only about 10% of Jane Foodie's sales are on the internet; the rest come from local retail stores, catering and her two cafes.
claims.argument: The claim is Jane Carroll's own statement about her sales mix. Fan and aggregator sites confirm that Jane Foodie sells flash-frozen foods online and in stores and has two cafes. None of them gives the online share of sales or mentions catering. The 10% figure rests only on her statement in the video, so it is neither confirmed nor contradicted.
claims.summary: No source confirms that online sales are only about 10%; only her own statement says so.

claims.text: Jane Foodie's soups have an average cost of $2.13, an MSRP of $6.50, and she sells them to the distributor for around $3.
claims.argument: A search summary of Shark Tank fan coverage repeats the same figures: frozen soup costs $2.13 to make, sells wholesale for about $3, and has a $6.50 MSRP. Jane Foodie (founder Jane Carroll) is a real Shark Tank company that sells soups, and the claim matches what the speaker said in the video. These are the founder's own statements, and no source contradicts them. Official company data was not found, so the figures rest on her statements and one secondary site.
claims.summary: Only one secondary site repeats the $2.13, $3 and $6.50 soup figures; no company source confirms them.

claims.text: Jane Foodie's soups have an average cost of $2.13 to make.
claims.argument: The claim repeats the founder's own statement about her costs. A Shark Tank recap site reports the same figures from her pitch: average cost to make frozen soup $2.13, wholesale $3, MSRP $6.50. No source contradicts these numbers. The figure is self-reported and no independent audit was found.
claims.summary: Jane Foodie's founder said soups cost $2.13 on average to make, and a Shark Tank recap repeats this.

claims.text: Jane Foodie's roasted parmesan cauliflower side dish costs 2.75 to make and has an MSRP of $850.
claims.argument: A Shark Tank blog write-up says Jane Foodie's roasted parm cauliflower costs $2.75 to make. It gives the MSRP as $8.50. The claim's $850 is almost certainly a transcription slip of "$8.50", but as written it is wrong by a factor of 100. The soup figures in the same source ($2.13 cost, $6.50 MSRP) match what the speaker said, so the source is consistent with the rest of the pitch. The only confirmation of the side-dish figures is a fan blog.
claims.summary: The cauliflower costs $2.75 to make, but it sells for $8.50, not $850.

claims.text: In 2023, Jane Foodie netted $24,000 from her two cafes.
claims.argument: The claim is a quote of what Jane Foodie said on Shark Tank. A Shark Tank recap says she made $24,000 through her two cafes in 2023, which matches the transcript. The figure is her own statement and no filing or audit backs it. Total company sales were far larger (reported around $640,000 in 2023), but that does not conflict with a $24,000 net from the cafes.
claims.summary: Only a fan blog recap repeats the $24,000 figure, so it is not independently checked.

claims.text: Jane Foodie's cafes serve flash frozen food that is heated, and the cafes have merchandised freezers.
claims.argument: Trade coverage describes Jane Foodie as a flash-frozen, ready-to-heat meal brand. Shark Tank summaries say she also has two cafes and sells in stores, which matches the founder's own statement that cafe food is flash frozen and heated. No independent source mentions freezers in the cafes, so that detail rests on her on-air statement. Nothing found contradicts it.
claims.summary: No independent source confirms the merchandised freezers inside the cafes.

claims.text: Jane Foodie does 45% of her sales in her cafes and 45% in the stores, and she is in about five local stores.
claims.argument: Jane Foodie is a real flash-frozen food brand, and trade coverage mentions a FreshDirect partnership. No retrieved source gives a sales split between cafes and stores, or a count of local stores. The claim is the founder's own statement about her business, and nothing found supports or contradicts it.
claims.summary: No source confirms the 45% cafe and 45% store split or the five local stores.

claims.text: Jane Foodie's cafes are about 450 square feet each.
claims.argument: Jane Foodie has cafes, including one at 28 Wells Ave in Yonkers and a planned one in Port Chester. No retrieved source states their square footage. The 450 sq ft figure is the founder's own statement in the video and could be neither confirmed nor contradicted. A Port Chester bank building was reported as the cafe site, which may suggest a larger space, but no size was given for the cafe.
claims.summary: No source gives the size of Jane Foodie's cafes, so 450 square feet is unconfirmed.

claims.text: Jane Foodie could manufacture centrally and drop the food off in freezers at small cafes or pop-up shops where it is heated, avoiding waste, which makes for a great business.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: Mark disagrees with Jane's strategy of going into retail for her flash frozen food company, Jane Foodie.
claims.argument: The episode context has Mark questioning Jane's plan to sell in the frozen section of grocery stores and calling her answer "bad." Fan sites say Mark Cuban opted out, one noting he thought the frozen business was too tied to her café. No retrieved written source quotes his objection to the retail strategy, so the claim rests mainly on the video transcript. Jane Foodie and Jane Carroll's Season 16 pitch are confirmed.
claims.summary: Written sources do not quote Mark's exact objection to the retail plan.

claims.text: Placing the product in grocery frozen sections requires finding shelf space, dealing with shipping, and expensive marketing because people won't immediately understand the product.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: Barbara offered $300,000 for 33% of Jane Foodie.
claims.argument: Shark Tank fan pages on Jane Foodie (Season 16) list Barbara Corcoran's opening offer as $300,000 for 33%. This matches the transcript, where she says "I'll make you an offer of $300,000 for 33%". Jane Carroll asked for $300,000 for 15%, and Lori Greiner won the deal at 25%. The sources are mostly fan-run sites, so confidence is slightly lower.
claims.summary: Barbara Corcoran did offer $300,000 for 33% of Jane Foodie on Shark Tank.

claims.text: The shark who offered $300K for 28% says she has many items in the freezer section (Pizza, Cupcake, B and Bagel, Frozen Farmer) that have collectively done over 150 million in sales.
claims.argument: Sources show the $300,000 for 28% offer on Jane Foodie came from Lori Greiner (Barbara Corcoran offered 33%), and Greiner is linked to Pizza Cupcake and Frozen Farmer. No retrieved reliable source gives a combined $150 million sales figure for her freezer brands. One low-quality site attributes such a figure to Fast Company, but it could not be checked. The "B and Bagel" item was also not identified.
claims.summary: Lori Greiner did offer $300K for 28%, but the $150 million frozen-food sales total was not confirmed.

claims.text: A shark offered $300K for 28% equity in Jane Foodie, undercutting Barbara's offer.
claims.argument: On Shark Tank Season 16, Episode 16, Barbara Corcoran offered $300,000 for 33% of Jane Foodie. Lori Greiner offered $300,000 for 28%, which undercut Barbara. The deal later closed with Lori at 25%. The speaker's "a shark" is Lori, and the claim is consistent with the episode recaps.
claims.summary: Lori Greiner offered $300K for 28%, which was lower than Barbara's 33% for the same money.

claims.text: Jane Foodie's negotiation ended with a shark countering at 27% after Jane asked about 25%, and another shark then offering 25%.
claims.argument: The transcript has Jane asking whether Barbara would accept 25%. Barbara answers "No, but I'll go with 27", and another shark (Lori) then says "I'll do 25". Summaries of the episode (Season 16) agree that Jane countered at 25% and Barbara suggested 27%. They also agree that Lori Greiner's $300,000 for 25% was the final deal. The sources are mostly fan-run blogs, and the 27% detail appears in only one of them. The transcript itself matches the claim.
claims.summary: Jane asked about 25%, Barbara said 27%, then Lori offered 25% and got the deal.

claims.text: Jane Foodie and Barbara settled the deal at 25% equity after Barbara asked whether Jane would accept 25%, Jane countered with 27%, and Barbara said she would do 25%.
claims.argument: Recaps of Season 16, Episode 16 say Jane Foodie sought $300,000 for 15%. Barbara offered 33%, and Jane countered at 25%. Barbara pushed back to 27%, and the final $300,000 for 25% deal was with Lori Greiner. That conflicts with the claim that Jane and Barbara settled at 25% after Jane countered with 27%. The sources are mostly fan blogs and none transcribes the episode, so some doubt remains.
claims.summary: Jane's 25% deal was with Lori Greiner, not Barbara, and Barbara was the one who pushed for 27%.

claims.text: Matt Gronberg and Sam Chason are seeking $250,000 for 5% of their company, Storage Scholars.
claims.argument: Coverage of the episode says the founders asked for $250,000 for 5%. Robert Herjavec then offered $500,000 for 20%, and Mark Cuban ended up investing $250,000 for 10%. The "25%" in the opening teaser is a separate negotiation exchange, not the ask. The 5% ask comes mostly from fan and aggregator sites, while CNBC confirms the $250,000 Cuban deal.
claims.summary: The founders did ask the Sharks for $250,000 for 5% of Storage Scholars.

claims.text: Storage Scholars customers pay a $50 fully refundable deposit and the company handles their entire college move-out.
claims.argument: Storage Scholars school pages show a $50 registration (listed as $49.99) that reserves space and includes the packing supply kit. The company also offers pickup and storage, which fits "handling the move-out". However, its own summary page says registration refunds are allowed only before supply kit shipment processing, which qualifies "fully refundable". A company blog says deposits are refundable, so the pitch is partly supported but the refund is conditional.
claims.summary: The roughly $50 sign-up payment and move-out help are real, but refunds only work before supplies ship.

claims.text: Storage Scholars has a partnership with students' universities to unlock their rooms once the campus is empty, and moves their belongings into storage for the summer.
claims.argument: Many universities (Wake Forest, FAU, Stetson, JMU, Skidmore, Elon, UC Davis) list Storage Scholars as an official or preferred partner. Some campuses allow contactless service, where movers enter on-campus housing to pick up belongings without the student there, and items go to storage over the summer. The claim is a slight generalization: access arrangements vary by school, and the "unlock once campus is empty" wording was not verified verbatim.
claims.summary: Storage Scholars does partner with many universities, and its movers can enter dorms to collect items for summer storage.

claims.text: All Storage Scholars moving is done by trained fellow students, creating high-paying jobs on campus.
claims.argument: Sources describing the company say its moves are staffed by students: more than 1,200 student workers in 2023-24, with about 400 more hired at peak times. Postings and a news profile cite pay of at least $15 an hour plus tips, with experienced staff earning up to roughly $25-27. That is above typical campus wages, so "high-paying" is plausible but is promotional wording. Training is mentioned in job postings. The claim that "all" moving is done by students could not be checked, and a SIRVA moving partnership exists.
claims.summary: No source confirms that every move is done only by students or that the pay is high compared with other campus jobs.

claims.text: The Storage Scholars founders built Storage Scholars in college, which allowed each of them to graduate debt-free.
claims.argument: Sam Chason and Matt Gronberg started Storage Scholars as students at Wake Forest. Coverage of their Shark Tank pitch and Wake Forest's giving site report that the company's early success let them graduate debt-free. The claim comes from the founders' own statement, and no independent check of their finances was found, but nothing contradicts it.
claims.summary: The founders did start the company at Wake Forest and say it let them graduate without debt.

claims.text: Storage Scholars operates on 23 college campuses, ranging from New York down to Texas.
claims.argument: Local coverage of the October 2022 Shark Tank episode reported Storage Scholars worked with 23 campuses in nine states. The company's campus lists include New York schools (NYU, Columbia, Skidmore) and Texas schools (UT Austin, TCU, Texas State), consistent with the "New York down to Texas" range. The company has since grown to far more campuses, but the claim reflects the pitch as made. The video is a rebroadcast, so the figure describes the 2022 pitch, not June 2026.
claims.summary: At the Shark Tank pitch in 2022, they said 23 campuses, and coverage then agrees.

claims.text: Storage Scholars started at Wake Forest University, the founders' alma mater, grew in the Carolinas and then spread to other colleges.
claims.argument: Sources say Sam Chason and Matt Gronberg started Storage Scholars in 2017 as Wake Forest students, in a dorm room, and both are Wake Forest alumni. The company later spread widely, to 48 schools by one report and 200+ campuses by the company's own site. No retrieved source explicitly describes the intermediate step of growing in the Carolinas first. It is plausible given the Wake Forest base and is the founders' own account.
claims.summary: Storage Scholars did start at Wake Forest, the founders' school, and later spread to many other colleges.

claims.text: The Storage Scholars service averages $559 in total, including boxes, tape and packing supplies, pickup, four months of storage, delivery, and $100 of complimentary insurance on every item.
claims.argument: Storage Scholars' pages say pricing covers pickup, storage and delivery, with free packing supplies. They also say every item has complimentary insurance up to $100. The $559 average appears only in a fan blog and in the founders' own statement. Third-party and company pages give varied ranges ($300–$500, $600–$800 for four months), so the average is neither confirmed nor contradicted.
claims.summary: The $559 average is only the founders' own figure; the included services and $100 insurance match company pages.

claims.text: Storage Scholars' costs per customer are about $199, including boxes, tape, packing supplies, labor and warehousing.
claims.argument: CNBC's report on the Storage Scholars Shark Tank pitch (aired October 2022) says all services, including labor, cost the company around $199 per move. Other outlets describe about $559 revenue against $199 in costs, which matches the speaker's "59 [559] revenue" and "$199 costs." The figure is the founders' own pitch claim from the Shark Tank appearance and was not independently audited. It may also be a 2022-era number rather than a current one.
claims.summary: Storage Scholars' founders did say it costs them about $199 per move, covering labor and storage.

claims.text: Storage Scholars is the only company the founders know of doing a full key access student storage system, and nobody else is doing key access with students and technology.
claims.argument: As a statement of what the founders know, it cannot be disproved. But the broader assertion that "nobody else" does key access is doubtful. Storage Squad has an exclusive Penn State partnership in which students pack, label and leave items in their rooms, and Box-n-Go and Collegeboxes run campus partnerships too. Storage Scholars' own comparison pages list rivals that offer door-to-door pickup. Whether any rival matches the exact combination of key access, student movers and custom technology could not be confirmed.
claims.summary: Founders say they know of no one else, but rivals like Storage Squad run similar pack-and-leave campus programs.

claims.text: Storage Scholars has a 4.8 star rating, which the founders attribute to their custom-built technology.
claims.argument: The claim is about what the founders say. Storage Scholars' own About page cites 4.8/5 from 3,500+ reviews, and secondary Shark Tank coverage reports a 4.8-star figure and a custom web app built by a founder's brother, a full-stack developer. Other figures differ: the 2025 offerings page shows 4.7, and Google reviews are reported around 4.5. The 4.8 figure is therefore company-reported and varies by source. The causal link to the technology is the founders' own explanation, not independently verified.
claims.summary: Independent sites show slightly lower ratings, so the 4.8 figure is only the company's own number.

claims.text: Storage Scholars' custom technology is a web app built over the last 6 years by Nick Poochie's brother, a full-stack developer.
claims.argument: Searches found Storage Scholars' founders named as Sam Chason and Matt Gronberg, with no mention of a "Nick Poochie". One aggregator-style summary says a founder's brother, a full-stack developer, built the web app over six years. That appears to repeat the video's transcript, not an independent source. The company's own pages describe a web portal and key access, but none names the developer or says whose brother he is. The claim's attribution to Nick Poochie's brother can be neither confirmed nor refuted.
claims.summary: No source confirms who built the app or that Nick Poochie's brother did.

claims.text: Storage Scholars does 3,300 moves across 23 campuses in nine states at the exact same week of the year.
claims.argument: Shark Tank recaps of the Season 14 pitch (October 2022) say the founders handled 3,300 moves on 23 campuses in the same week, and that the company served 23 schools across nine states from the East Coast to Texas. The claim matches that pitch. The company's own site now says 200+ campuses and 100,000+ moves, so the figures are a 2022 snapshot, not current numbers. The nine-state detail rests on a single secondary recap rather than a primary document.
claims.summary: The nine-state detail was only found in one recap, and current figures differ.

claims.text: Wake Forest University costs $70,000 a year, and Anthony Poochie was looking at over $100,000 in student loans.
claims.argument: Wake Forest's official 2025-26 figures list tuition and fees at $70,332, so "$70,000" fits tuition, but the full cost of attendance is $94,600. Storage Scholars was founded at Wake Forest by Sam Chason with Matt Gronberg, and no source mentions an "Anthony Poochie". The "over $100,000 in loans" is the speaker's own account of what he faced and could not be independently verified. Chason has said the business let him graduate debt-free.
claims.summary: Wake Forest tuition is about $70,000, but the total is near $94,600, and no source names Anthony Poochie.

claims.text: By the end of its first year at Wake Forest, Storage Scholars serviced 64 customers and had $18,000 in revenue.
claims.argument: A Wake Forest giving story says the first-year offering drew 64 customers and produced $18,000 in revenue. Shark Tank recaps repeat the same numbers. Sources differ on whether the company started in 2016 or 2017, but that does not affect the first-year figures.
claims.summary: Sources say the first year brought 64 customers and $18,000 in revenue, as he says.

claims.text: The founders started the business while at school and paid off over $100,000 in student debt.
claims.argument: Storage Scholars began in Sam Chason's freshman dorm at Wake Forest, and Matt Gronberg joined soon after. Wake Forest News and the Shark Tank Blog say the business let them graduate debt-free. One source puts Gronberg's expected loans at about $100,000. The "over $100,000" total is the founders' own account and no independent record of it was found, so the figure carries some uncertainty.
claims.summary: The exact amount of debt paid off, over $100,000, rests only on the founders' own statements.

claims.text: Anthony Poochie worked 106 hours in 7 days unloading trucks until 4 in the morning.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: The Storage Scholars ownership split is 70/30 and the founders have taken in zero dollars from outside investors.
claims.argument: Secondary sources about the 2022 Shark Tank pitch say Sam Chason holds 70% and Matt Gronberg 30%. They also say the company had no outside investors and the founders worked on it full time. Those statements apply to the time before the pitch: Mark Cuban then took 10% for $250,000. No primary document confirms the exact split, but nothing contradicts it, and it matches what the founders said on air.
claims.summary: The 70/30 split rests on secondary blogs, with no company filing to confirm it.

claims.text: Storage Scholars has done $1.826 million in sales this year.
claims.argument: News 12 and Shark Tank Blog report the $1.826 million sales figure for Storage Scholars from its October 2022 Shark Tank pitch. NBC reports a similar $1.86 million for 2022 revenue. So the speaker's number matches the pitch, where "this year" meant 2022. The video was uploaded in June 2026, and later figures were much higher (reports of $5 million or more). The claim is accurate only as a quote from the pitch, not as current sales. News 12 describes the figure as "last year", so the exact period is slightly unclear.
claims.summary: Reports differ on whether the figure was for 2022 or the year before.

claims.text: Storage Scholars does about 700 students of summer storage at Wake Forest University.
claims.argument: Storage Scholars was founded at Wake Forest and the school is its largest, with a reported figure of about 700 students using the service. That number appears in coverage tied to the founders' earlier Shark Tank pitch, so it matches what the founders say. No independent 2026 source confirms the exact count, so it rests on the founders' own statement.
claims.summary: No current source confirms the 700-student summer storage count at Wake Forest for this year.

claims.text: At SMU, a school outside the Carolinas in Texas, Storage Scholars had 269 customers.
claims.argument: Shark Tank recaps state that SMU was Storage Scholars' newest school outside the Carolinas, with 269 customers, and that Wake Forest was the biggest at about 700 students. This matches the pitch, which also cites $1.826 million in sales. The figure comes from the show's pitch and secondary recaps, not from company records.
claims.summary: Storage Scholars did report 269 customers at SMU in Texas during its Shark Tank pitch.

claims.text: Storage Scholars grows at its schools through partnerships with universities, which email customers on its behalf and put it on the university website, which drives SEO.
claims.argument: Wake Forest, SMU and UC Davis publicly list Storage Scholars as an official, partner or preferred provider. Wake Forest's parent and mail-services pages promote it, which matches "on the university website". The sources found do not directly confirm that universities send emails for it or that the listings drive SEO. Those points are the founder's own account of how the company grows, and nothing contradicts them.
claims.summary: No source directly confirms that universities email customers for it or that this drives SEO.

claims.text: Kevin offered $250,000 for 20% equity in Storage Scholars.
claims.argument: The transcript has the speaker saying "I'll do the 250 for 20%" after the founders asked for $250,000 for 5%. Search summaries about the Season 14 episode (aired Oct 14, 2022) say Kevin O'Leary made the first offer, $250,000 for 20%, and Daymond John matched it. Mark Cuban's deal later closed at $250,000 for 10%. One recap that describes a different O'Leary offer conflicts, but it appears to be an outlier. The retrieved pages were search snippets, not full articles.
claims.summary: Kevin O'Leary did offer $250,000 for 20% of Storage Scholars, as the transcript shows.

claims.text: Damon offered $250,000 for 20% equity in Storage Scholars, matching Kevin's offer.
claims.argument: The speaker's own quote has the Shark saying "I'll match Kevin 250 for 20%". A search summary of the Season 14, Episode 4 recap pages says Kevin O'Leary offered $250,000 for 20% and Daymond John matched it. The name "Damon" is just a spelling of Daymond. Mark Cuban's $250,000 offer was the one the founders accepted, reportedly for about 10%. Support for the order of offers comes from secondary recap pages that partly conflict with each other, so confidence is not higher.
claims.summary: Daymond John did match Kevin's offer of $250,000 for 20% in Storage Scholars.

claims.text: Robert offered $500,000 for 20% equity in Storage Scholars.
claims.argument: Coverage of the Season 14 episode says Robert Herjavec offered $500,000 for 20% equity, double the $250,000 the founders asked for. Kevin O'Leary and Daymond John each offered $250,000 for 20%. The founders took Mark Cuban's offer of $250,000 instead. This matches the quoted transcript.
claims.summary: Robert Herjavec did offer $500,000 for 20% of Storage Scholars on Shark Tank.

claims.text: Kevin and Damon offered a joint deal of $250,000 each for a combined 40% equity in Storage Scholars.
claims.argument: In the episode (Season 14, Episode 4), Kevin O'Leary and Daymond John first each offered $250,000 for 20%. Robert Herjavec then countered with $500,000 for 20%. In the quoted transcript, Daymond says "Kevin and I will give you 250 a piece for 40%", which is the joint offer the claim describes. A Sportskeeda article describes this as a combined $500,000 for 40% offer from the two. The name "Damon" is a transcript spelling of Daymond John.
claims.summary: Kevin and Daymond teamed up, offering $250,000 each, $500,000 total, for 40% of the company.

claims.text: Mark offered $250,000 for 12% of Storage Scholars.
claims.argument: Search summaries of the Season 14, Episode 4 coverage say Mark Cuban opened with $250,000 for 12%, citing his school connections. The founders then negotiated and the final deal was $250,000 for 10%. The claim concerns only the initial offer, which matches the speaker's own transcript. The 12% figure was seen only in search summaries and a Sportskeeda snippet, so confidence is slightly lower.
claims.summary: Mark's first offer was $250,000 for 12%; the deal later settled at 10%.

claims.text: Mark said that he has a platform and connections to schools, and that if he starts talking about Storage Scholars, the phone will ring for them to open up new schools, though maybe not all of them will be partner schools.
claims.argument: CNBC's 2022 report on the Shark Tank episode quotes Cuban saying "I've got a platform", "There's schools that I have connections to" and "the phone's going to ring for you to open up new schools". The speaker's rendering from captions matches these words and the sense of the offer pitch. The "maybe they won't all be partner schools" aside is not in the CNBC excerpts but fits the episode exchange.
claims.summary: Mark Cuban really said this when pitching his offer to the Storage Scholars founders on Shark Tank.

quote.author: Mark
quote.quoted_text: I've got a platform and, you know, there schools that I have connections to and if I get out there starting to talk about it, maybe they won't all be partner schools, but you're the phone's going to ring for you to open up new schools.
quote.original_quote: I've got a platform. … There's schools that I have connections to … the phone's going to ring for you to open up new schools.
quote.context: Mark Cuban's offer to Storage Scholars founders on Shark Tank Season 14 (aired October 14, 2022): $250K, with an argument that his platform and school connections add value. CNBC reported the lines in 2022. The speaker's use matches.

claims.text: Mark has been very outspoken about college debt.
claims.argument: Mark Cuban has repeatedly commented publicly on student debt. He called taking on massive student loans "the dumbest thing you can do," opposed blanket forgiveness, and promoted community college as a cheaper route. CNBC notes he has argued for plans to lower student debt. The Storage Scholars founders also said on Shark Tank that they knew college debt was a big issue for him.
claims.summary: Mark Cuban has indeed spoken out often about college debt and student loans.

claims.text: Storage Scholars received four offers from the sharks and countered Mark with a request for $350,000 for 8%.
claims.argument: Reports say Storage Scholars, which asked for $250,000 for 5%, got offers from four Sharks. Mark Cuban's offer was $250,000 for 12%, and the deal ended at $250,000 for 10%. The "$350,000 for 8%" counter appears in the quoted transcript ("Would you be willing to do 350 for 8%"). Written recaps are inconsistent about it, and some say 10%. The transcript is the direct source for what was said on air, so the claim matches it. Mark answered that he would do 10%.
claims.summary: They got four offers and asked Mark for $350,000 for 8%, then settled at $250,000 for 10%.

claims.text: Storage Scholars and Mark agreed to a deal of $250,000 for 10% equity.
claims.argument: CNBC and other outlets report that Storage Scholars founders Sam Chason and Matt Gronberg took a $250,000 Shark Tank deal with Mark Cuban for 10% equity. The negotiation in the transcript matches the reports: the founders countered with $350K for 8% and $300K for 10%, and Mark held at $250K for 10%. One outlet (Sportskeeda) says 12%, but that is an outlier.
claims.summary: Storage Scholars and Mark Cuban did agree on $250,000 for 10%.

claims.text: Mike Su from Springfield, Missouri, pitched his company Step, seeking $300,000 for a 3% stake.
claims.argument: Springfield Business Journal and other sources report that Mike Sewell of StepNpull, a Springfield, Missouri company, went on Shark Tank seeking $300,000 for 3% equity. He pitched on behalf of his two partners, Ron Ely and Kelly Coddington. The claim's "Mike Su" and "Step" match the video's auto-caption of "Mike Sewell" and "StepNpull". These are transcription slips, not a different person or company. Kevin O'Leary offered $300,000 for 6%, which is not part of this claim.
claims.summary: The pitch was real, but the man is Mike Sewell and the company is StepNpull.

claims.text: Step and Pull is a small device that mounts on the bottom of a commercial latchless door and lets people pull the door open with their foot.
claims.argument: Manufacturer and retailer pages describe StepNpull as a small plate mounted at the bottom of commercial latchless doors. A user places a foot on it and pulls the door open, avoiding the handle. The speaker's wording closely matches the product description ("attaches to any commercial latch less door and gives the user the option of pulling the door open with their foot"). The sources are mostly seller pages, but they directly describe the product.
claims.summary: StepNpull is a small foot-operated door puller for latchless commercial doors, as described.

claims.text: Door handles are a common touch point that harbor bacteria.
claims.argument: Studies of hospitals and public restrooms repeatedly find bacteria on door handles. A Liverpool hospital study found Staphylococcus on 43% to 65% of handles. A Lebanese study found 93.8% of restroom handles and knobs contaminated with potentially pathogenic bacteria. A hotel study showed door handles among the most contaminated high-touch surfaces. The claim is a general one, and the evidence supports it. It does not say how often handles cause illness.
claims.summary: Studies find bacteria on door handles, which many people touch every day.

claims.text: Step and Pull can be installed in office buildings, restaurant patio doors or clean room environments for health care professionals.
claims.argument: StepNpull is a foot-operated opener that mounts on latchless commercial doors. Retailer listings name offices, restaurants/food service and hospital or healthcare facilities as suitable places. Patio doors and clean rooms were not specifically named in the sources retrieved, but they are latchless-door settings consistent with the product's stated use. The claim is a reasonable marketing-style description of where it can be installed.
claims.summary: No source names patio doors or clean rooms specifically as install locations.

claims.text: The COVID-19 pandemic has triggered hyper awareness of germs globally.
claims.argument: Global surveys show that the pandemic raised hygiene awareness and handwashing in many countries. YouGov and Imperial College tracked 29 territories, and about 80% reported frequent handwashing in 2021. An 11-nation survey found half of respondents changed at least one behaviour. A UConn study linked germ aversion to COVID concern and preventive behaviour. "Hyper awareness" is a loose, informal phrase, and most of the data is self-reported, but the substance is well supported.
claims.summary: COVID-19 really did make people around the world much more aware of germs and hygiene.

claims.text: There are similar products to Step and Pull, but Step and Pull's design is patented.
claims.argument: US patent 9,115,530 B2, titled "Step and pull sanitary door opener," exists and describes stepping on a device and pulling the foot back to open the door. It also cites earlier similar devices, such as the "Sanitary Door Opener" application US 2005/0005402, and a later foot-operated opener application, so similar products exist. Several Shark Tank coverage pages say the founders patented the design. One caveat is that the retailer pages do not name the patent number.
claims.summary: The door opener has a real US patent, and similar foot-operated openers exist.

claims.text: Step and Pull is low cost to manufacture because of its design.
claims.argument: The StepNpull is a simple serrated aluminum piece, made in Missouri. Regional business coverage describes the founders' pitch as an easy-to-manufacture, inexpensive design, and one source puts bulk cost under $20. A less reliable site says about $8–9 per unit against a $29.95 retail price. Retail listings of roughly $15–35 fit a low-cost product. The claim is the founders' own pitch, and no primary cost breakdown was found, so the exact link between the design and the low cost rests on secondary sources.
claims.summary: No primary cost figure was confirmed; only secondary reports describe the design as cheap to make.

claims.text: Step and Pull's business is in its 13th year, run by Mike Su and his two partners, who had full-time jobs and ran it as a sideline business.
claims.argument: StepNpull was founded in 2007 by Mike Sewell, Kelly Coddington and Ron Ely, former telecom colleagues, and began as a side project. The "Mike Su" in the claim is almost certainly a caption error for Sewell. The Shark Tank pitch was in 2021, and the company reportedly sold more in March 2020 than in the previous 13 years combined. That fits a "13th year" statement. The full-time-jobs detail is consistent with the side-project origin, though it was not directly confirmed in the sources retrieved.
claims.summary: The exact "13th year" count was not directly checked against a primary source.

claims.text: In the first five years Step and Pull's sales were fairly flat, with maybe $35,000 sold.
claims.argument: Secondary summaries repeat that StepNpull's first years were a flat side business and that about $35,000 was sold before the March 2020 surge (reported as $1.7 million in March 2020). None of them gives a separate five-year total, and some describe the $35,000 as covering a longer span. An SBJ article gives 2019 revenue as $336,000, which suggests growth in the years after the flat period. The figure therefore matches the founder's own pitch but cannot be independently confirmed or contradicted.
claims.summary: Flat early sales are reported, but no source independently confirms the $35,000 figure for the first five years.

claims.text: Step and Pull sold more in March than in the whole time it has been in business, about a million dollars.
claims.argument: Coverage of StepNpull's founder says March 2020 sales exceeded everything the company had sold in its prior 13 years, so the core "more than the whole time in business" holds. The reported March figure is about $1.7 million, though, not "about a million". The $7 million year-to-date figure matches reports. The "$35,000" early-sales figure is also questionable, since 2019 revenue alone was reported at $336,000. Sources are mostly local news and fan blogs, with no primary document.
claims.summary: March 2020 sales did beat all earlier sales, but they were about $1.7 million, not about $1 million.

claims.text: Step and Pull's year-to-date sales are approaching $7 million.
