claims.argument: The pitch appears to be the Shark Tank segment, which aired in April 2021. The founder's "this year" refers to 2020, when pandemic demand pushed sales up. Reporting says about $35,000 in lifetime sales before the pandemic, $1.7 million in March 2020 alone, and roughly $7 million for 2020 (one later report says $8 million). This matches the claim as made in the pitch. Nothing found shows $7 million year to date in 2026, so the claim only holds for the pitch's own time frame.
claims.summary: No source confirms $7 million in year-to-date sales for 2026 itself.

claims.text: Step and Pull retails for $29.95.
claims.argument: Ferguson lists the StepNpull foot door opener at $29.95, and a Shark Tank follow-up site says it sells for $29.95. Other sellers show $34.95 (Staples), $29.99 or $25.95, so actual prices vary by seller. The speaker is the company's own representative, and $29.95 as a suggested retail price fits the listings found.
claims.summary: Store prices vary, so no official list price was directly confirmed.

claims.text: Step and Pull's US cost to manufacture is between $8 and $9, and one manufacturer in southwest Missouri got the price down under $7.
claims.argument: Shark Tank fan sites report that StepNpull retails for $29.95 and that its US manufacturing cost is $8 to $9 per unit. This matches the pitch. The company is based in southwest Missouri (Springfield and Fair Grove) and is made there, so a southwest Missouri manufacturer is plausible. No independent source confirms the "under seven" price. That detail rests on the founder's own statement. The sales figures around the pitch (about $7 million in 2020) are consistent with Missouri business reporting.
claims.summary: No independent source confirms the sub-$7 price from the Missouri manufacturer.

claims.text: About 25% of Step and Pull's business is distributors and 75% is direct.
claims.argument: The speaker, StepNpull's founder, gives the split himself, and a recap of the Shark Tank pitch reports the same figures: 25% distributors and 75% direct, with about 35% of sales through the website. That recap is a single secondary source, and the figure dates from the 2021 pitch. No official data or independent reporting confirms the split. Later coverage says distribution partners and retailers such as Lowe's and Amazon were added, so the current share is unknown. Nothing contradicts the claim, but it rests on the company's own statement.
claims.summary: Only the founder's own words give this 25/75 split, and no independent source confirms it.

claims.text: Step and Pull's website is its highest sales channel, at over 30%, probably 35%, of its sales.
claims.argument: The searches turned up no company filing or independent report on StepNpull's sales by channel. The only related item is a fan site, sharktanktalks.com. It says 25% of sales are distributors and 75% direct, with about 35% of the direct sales through the website. That is a different and older breakdown from the claim, and it is unverified. The claim is the founder's own self-reported figure, so it is neither confirmed nor refuted.
claims.summary: No independent source confirms how much of StepNpull's sales come from its website.

claims.text: Mr. Wonderful (Kevin O'Leary) said the most valuable asset we can never own is our time, and that the one asset more valuable than any dollar you will ever earn is your time and your ability to enjoy it.
claims.argument: Searches found no page with the exact wording "most valuable asset we can never own" or "more valuable than any dollar you will ever earn" from O'Leary. Articles do show him repeatedly saying time is an entrepreneur's most valuable asset. The words in the video look like his own on-air remarks to the founder, but no transcript of that episode was retrieved to confirm them.
claims.summary: The exact words were not found, though O'Leary often says time is his most valuable asset.

quote.author: Mr. Wonderful
quote.quoted_text: the most valuable asset we can never own [music] is our time.

claims.text: One shark said he has a fully automated factory in New York in which he is a partner, so he could probably reduce Step and Pull's costs and increase its sales.
claims.argument: StepNpull pitched on Shark Tank season 12, episode 19 (2021), with offers from Kevin O'Leary, Daymond John and Lori Greiner. Recaps mention Daymond saying he can lower production costs and an International Door Association idea. None of the retrieved pages has the automated New York factory line or says which shark said it. The speaker's unnamed "shark" therefore cannot be checked.
claims.summary: The episode's pitch is real, but no transcript confirming these exact words or which shark said them was found.

quote.author: Shark (partner in a fully automated factory in New York)
quote.quoted_text: I also have a a fully automated factory uh in [music] New York that I'm a partner in. So, I can reduce your cost probably and I can also increase your sales.

claims.text: Lori offered $300,000 for 5% equity in Step and Pull, plus a royalty of 50 cents per unit, dropping to 20 cents per unit once 500,000 units are reached.
claims.argument: A Shark Tank recap says Lori offered $300,000 for 5% plus a 50 cent royalty, dropping to 20 cents per unit. It frames the threshold as recouping $500,000, while the speaker's words say "once I've hit 500,000", which is ambiguous. No transcript of Lori's own words was retrieved, so the wording cannot be compared exactly.
claims.summary: Lori's offer matches a recap of the episode, but her exact words were not found.

quote.author: Lori
quote.quoted_text: I would do $300,000 for 5% equity. I would want um 50 cents back a unit and then once I've hit 500,000 then the royalty will drop to 20 cents per.

claims.text: Mike accepted Kevin's offer of $300,000 for 6% equity in Step and Pull, rejecting the other shark's offer of $300,000 for 8%.
claims.argument: Summaries of the April 2021 Shark Tank episode (Season 12) say Mike Sewell of StepNpull took Kevin O'Leary's $300,000 for 6% equity offer. Daymond John had offered 8%, and Kevin lowered his ask to 6%. The video transcript agrees: Mike says "Kevin, let's do it." The deal reportedly never closed after the show, but the claim is only about the on-air decision. The other shark is not named in the claim, so the claim is consistent with the sources.
claims.summary: Mike took Kevin's $300,000 for 6% offer on the show, turning down the 8% offer.

claims.text: Neil Cameron, Peter Ferrer and Dennis Lionady are seeking $250,000 for a 20% equity stake in their company Nuts and More.
claims.argument: Nuts 'N More pitched on Shark Tank Season 4, Episode 18 (2013), asking $250,000 for 20% equity. The founders are listed as Neil Cameron, Dennis Iannotti and Peter Ferreira. "Ferrer" and "Lionady" look like auto-transcript misspellings of those names, which is not a substantive error. The company name and the ask match.
claims.summary: They did ask for $250,000 for 20%; the names are just spelled differently in the transcript.

claims.text: Nuts and More are fortified butters with added protein and added omegas, high in fiber with no sugar added.
claims.argument: This is a quote from the Shark Tank pitch (Season 4). Sources describe Nuts 'N More as fortified peanut and almond butters with added whey protein and flax for omega-3s. They list about 2–3 g fiber per serving and about 1 g sugar. One source summarizes it as "high in fiber, no added sugar". Some flavors use xylitol as a sweetener, and "high in fiber" is the pitch's own wording. The claim is a fair description of the product as marketed.
claims.summary: The pitch describes the product as the sources do: protein and omega added, fiber, no added sugar.

claims.text: Nuts and More was born this past year in a small corner of the presenter's family's bakery shop.
claims.argument: The claim repeats what the presenter (Peter Ferreira) said in the Shark Tank pitch, and that line is in the quoted transcript. Reports say Nuts 'N More began in the back of his family's small bakery shop, and that production started in Peter's family bakery. "This past year" refers to the time of the original pitch (Season 4). Founding-year reports vary (2010 or 2011), so that detail is not firmly confirmed. The video was uploaded in 2026, but the pitch itself is older.
claims.summary: The exact founding year behind "this past year" is not confirmed.

claims.text: Nuts and More has four varieties: peanut butter, chocolate peanut butter, almond butter and chocolate almond butter, fortified with protein and flax.
claims.argument: Retailer and history pages list Nuts 'N More's original products as peanut butter, chocolate peanut butter, almond butter and chocolate almond butter. They describe these spreads as fortified with whey protein and flax. The brand later added many more flavors, such as cinnamon raisin almond butter and cookie butter. The claim is therefore accurate for the line as pitched, and no longer describes the full range. The sources are third-party retailer pages, not the original episode transcript or the brand's own site.
claims.summary: The exact count of four flavors at pitch time is not shown by a primary source.

claims.text: Nuts and More almond butter has 14 grams of protein per serving compared to seven grams in peanut butter, and the flax seed provides omegas 3, 6 and 9 and added fiber.
claims.argument: Grocery listings (Ralphs, QFC, Mariano's) show Nuts 'N More High Protein Almond Butter at 12g protein per serving, and another listing says 11g. The 14g number appears in marketing bullet points and in some listings for other flavors. The flax claim holds: the product uses flax for added omega-3s and protein. The omega 3-6-9 wording appears in listings for the brand's peanut butter. The 14g versus 7g comparison is therefore somewhat overstated against the label.
claims.summary: The almond butter's label shows about 12g protein, not 14g, though flax and omegas are real.

verdict_reasons.name: Scale larger than in the sources
verdict_reasons.definition: A number or scale in the speech is larger than the check found.

evidence.text: you got 14 grams of protein compared to seven per serving.

verdict_reasons.explanation: Said «14 grams of protein compared to seven per serving», while the label in the check shows about 12 g for the almond butter.

claims.text: Nuts and More has been valued by its founders at $1.25 million.
claims.argument: Shark Tank coverage says the Nuts 'N More founders asked for $250,000 for 20% equity. That implies a $1.25 million valuation. Another source also states the founders valued the company at $1.25 million. The final deal was $250,000 for 35%, but that is the negotiated outcome and does not change the founders' own valuation.
claims.summary: The founders asked $250,000 for 20%, which values the company at $1.25 million.

claims.text: Nuts and More started selling about 5 months ago and has $100,000 in sales to date.
claims.argument: Recaps of the Nuts 'N More Shark Tank pitch (Season 4, aired 2013) say the founders asked for $250,000 for 20%, a $1.25 million valuation. They had reached $100,000 in sales in about five months. This matches the speaker's statement. The sources are mostly secondary blogs and news sites, not the episode itself. The nine-warehouse detail was not found, but it is not part of this claim.
claims.summary: Reports on the Shark Tank pitch match: about $100,000 in sales in the first five months.

claims.text: The founders say Nuts and More was approached by the country's largest national distributor, which has nine warehouses across the country; a pallet in each would be a little over a million in revenue.
claims.argument: The claim reports what the founders said in their pitch, and the transcript shows they said it. Shark Tank pages for Nuts 'N More (Season 4) agree with the pitch's framing: $250,000 for 20% implies a $1.25 million valuation, and about $100K in sales to date. They also mention a purchase order or interest from a large distributor that the company needed cash to fulfil. No retrieved source independently confirms the nine warehouses or the "little over a million" pallet figure. That is the founders' own projection, and the claim only says the founders said it.
claims.summary: No outside source confirms the nine warehouses or the pallet math.

claims.text: The distributor has not ordered because Nuts and More cannot fulfill the order.
claims.argument: The claim repeats the founder's own answer in the pitch: the distributor has not ordered because the company can't fulfill. The searches turned up only coverage of a different, earlier "Nuts 'N More" pitch from 2013. That pitch also involved a large distributor order the founders needed cash to fulfill. No independent source covers the 2026 pitch, the nine-warehouse distributor, or whether an order was placed. The claim is a self-reported business statement that can't be checked independently.
claims.summary: Only the founder says the distributor hasn't ordered because he can't fulfill; no outside source confirms it.

claims.text: Nuts and More peanut butter retails for $10.99 and almond butter for $12.99.
claims.argument: No retrieved source lists Nuts 'N More peanut butter at $10.99 or almond butter at $12.99. Retailer listings for the brand's high-protein peanut spreads showed other prices ($12.00 sale, $17.95, $19.49, $20.96), and Business Insider gave "from $11.99". Prices differ by flavor, size and seller. The figures come from the pitcher's own statement, so they could be their own retail or direct-to-consumer prices for a different product line. The sources found neither confirm nor rule that out.
claims.summary: No source confirms the $10.99 and $12.99 prices; retailer prices found were different.

claims.text: Nuts and More makes the peanut butter for $2.90 and the almond butter for $4.
claims.argument: The $2.90 and $4 figures are the founder's own pitch statement about unit cost. Searches of Shark Tank recaps and company coverage found no independent source giving Nuts 'N More's cost per jar. Nothing contradicts the figures either. Coverage found mostly concerns the older 2013 Season 4 appearance, not the 2026 pitch.
claims.summary: No outside source confirms the $2.90 and $4 cost per jar; it is only the founder's own statement.

claims.text: With the investment, Nuts and More could buy raw materials at higher volume, which would bring the price of its peanut butter down $1.50.
claims.argument: No fact check available — this is a prediction about the future, which no source can confirm yet.

claims.text: Nuts and More is sold in 32 retail outlets, out of 35,000.
claims.argument: The claim repeats what the founder said in the pitch, and no outside source confirms or contradicts the 32-outlet count or the 35,000 total. Coverage of Nuts 'N More's Shark Tank episode (Season 4, 2013) gives the terms ($250,000 for 20%, about a $1.25 million valuation) but no early store count. Later articles report roughly 1,800 stores, which is a much later period and does not refute a figure from the pitch. As the speaker's own statement of his distribution at the time, it is plausible but unverified.
claims.summary: No source confirms the 32-outlet figure; it comes only from the pitch itself.

claims.text: About 50% of Nuts and More's business is online.
claims.argument: The 50% figure is the founder's own answer during the pitch, and the searches found no company filing or reliable report that splits sales between online and retail. Secondary articles mention online sales (Amazon, QVC, the company website) and give shaky revenue estimates of $6–7 million a year. None gives an online percentage. The claim can't be confirmed or refuted from what was retrieved.
claims.summary: No independent source confirms that about half of Nuts and More's sales are online.

claims.text: Nuts and More sells about 70 units a month from most stores, and the stores keep reordering every week.
claims.argument: The claim is a Shark's summary of the pitch, and the founder answered "Absolutely." Outside sources say Nuts 'N More pitched in 2013 and that retailers were already buying and reordering. They also report about $100,000 in sales over the first five months. None gives a per-store figure such as 70 units a month or weekly reorders. The sources give no evidence for or against these numbers, so they stay unverified founder claims.
claims.summary: No source confirms the 70-units-a-month figure; it is only the founder's on-air agreement.

claims.text: The Nuts and More valuation is too high because it assumes the company has already landed the big distributor orders it has not yet fulfilled.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: Nuts and More currently makes its jar for $2.90, and the jar initially cost $4.
claims.argument: The claim repeats the founder's own statement in the pitch about production cost per jar. Searches confirmed the pitch itself ($250,000 ask, Robert Herjavec and Mark Cuban deal) but found no source giving the cost to make a jar, then or now. The figures are the founder's unverified statement about internal costs, so they can be neither confirmed nor refuted.
claims.summary: No outside source gives the jar's making cost of $2.90 or the earlier $4.

claims.text: Nuts and More processes, assembles and packages its products in-house itself.
claims.argument: Local news coverage describes Nuts 'N More filling jars at its own factory in Pawtucket, Rhode Island. Other sources say it moved from a 1,000 sq ft production space to a 10,000 sq ft facility, which fits in-house production. No source states that an outside co-packer is used, but none explicitly confirms that every step (processing, assembly, packaging) is done in-house. The claim is what the founder said in the pitch, and the available evidence is consistent with it.
claims.summary: No source clearly states whether every step is done in-house rather than by an outside maker.

claims.text: When Nuts and More started the brand, fitness professionals such as bodybuilders and bikini competitors came to the founders.
claims.argument: Brand and retail profiles say the founders were fitness and nutrition experts who wanted fortified nut butters for themselves and their clients. The brand markets to the fitness crowd, with bodybuilder photos on its social pages. No retrieved source describes bodybuilders or bikini competitors approaching the founders at the start. The claim is a plausible founder anecdote from the pitch, but it is not independently verified.
claims.summary: The founders' fitness roots fit, but no source confirms bodybuilders or bikini competitors came to them.

claims.text: The Nuts and More founders priced their offer at $250,000 for the investment ask, which a shark called a shame given the great packaging and name.
claims.argument: Sources say Nuts 'N More asked for $250,000 for 20% equity on Shark Tank (Season 4, Episode 18). Barbara Corcoran is reported to have praised the great name and stellar packaging before leaving over the high valuation. The exact "what a shame" wording was not found in the written recaps, but it fits the described scene. The shark's complaint is strictly about the valuation implied by the $250,000-for-20% ask, which the claim simplifies.
claims.summary: The exact "what a shame" wording was not found in written sources.

claims.text: For Barbara to give Nuts and More $250,000, she would have to take 80% of the business.
claims.argument: Recaps say Nuts 'N More asked $250,000 for 20% and Barbara Corcoran went out over the valuation. Cuban and Herjavec later took 35%. No retrieved source has Barbara saying she would need 80%. The quoted lines sit next to a remark about a face cream priced at $250,000, so the "80%" may belong to that pitch rather than Nuts and More. This could not be settled without a transcript.
claims.summary: No source confirms Barbara said she'd need 80% for Nuts and More; the quote may be from another pitch.

claims.text: The wholesale price of Nuts and More peanut product is $5.75 and the almond product is $7.25.
claims.argument: The figures come from the founder's own statement during the pitch. Retailer pages (RangeMe, Faire) hide wholesale prices behind sign-up and show only retail prices of about $10 to $16. No source gives wholesale prices for the peanut or almond product that either confirm or contradict $5.75 and $7.25.
claims.summary: No source shows the $5.75 and $7.25 wholesale prices, so they could not be checked.

claims.text: The Nuts and More founders say they need about $7,000 to buy enough peanuts to bring their costs down to where they want them.
claims.argument: The quoted exchange has a Shark asking for the total needed to get prices down to the target. The founder answers "About um $7,000", and another speaker adds "For peanuts", so the claim matches that dialogue. Searches confirmed the Nuts 'N More Shark Tank context, including the $250,000 ask, the 35% deal with Cuban and Herjavec, and the $75,000 upfront with $175,000 held for future orders. None of them mentions the $7,000 peanut figure, so it is supported only by the transcript excerpt itself and no independent source.
claims.summary: No retrieved source repeats the $7,000 peanut figure, so it rests on the video's own wording.

claims.text: The Nuts and More founders say that with $50,000 they could fulfill the distributor's purchase order, lower their price point and take orders.
claims.argument: The episode coverage confirms Nuts 'N More pitched with a large distributor purchase order that needed cash to fulfill, and the sharks later offered $250,000 for 35%. In the quoted exchange, the founder agrees that spending $50,000 lets him fulfill that one order, make a little money and get volume going. The "lower price point and take orders" part comes from a Shark (Robert) stating it, and the founder confirms it ("Absolutely"). The attribution is slightly loose, but the substance holds. No source retrieved gave the $50,000 line directly, so it rests on the transcript.
claims.summary: The exact $50,000 exchange is not confirmed by a written source; only the transcript and general episode coverage were available.

claims.text: Mark proposed $250,000 for 35% of Nuts and More, with a contingency of $75,000 in cash upfront and the balance where and when needed.
claims.argument: Show recaps report the final Nuts 'N More deal as $250,000 for 35%. It had $75,000 upfront to fill a large order, and the remaining $175,000 was available to fund future purchase orders. Mark held at 35% while Robert had first said 50%, which fits the transcript. One older list gives a different figure (18% for $125,000), but it conflicts with the other accounts and looks like an error.
claims.summary: Mark offered $250,000 for 35%, with $75,000 upfront and the rest as needed.

claims.text: Robert offered $250,000 for 50% of Nuts and More.
claims.argument: Coverage of the Shark Tank episode says Herjavec offered $250,000 for a 50% stake in Nuts 'N More. Cuban offered $250,000 for 35%, with $75,000 upfront. Herjavec then joined Cuban's 35% deal. This matches the speaker's own words in the context: "I was going to offer you 250,000 for 50%". The sources are mostly secondary blogs, but they agree on the core terms.
claims.summary: Robert Herjavec did offer $250,000 for 50% of Nuts 'N More, before joining Mark's 35% deal.

claims.text: One of the sharks said that 50% would create more problems than it solves because the two sharks would hold 16% each and would get resentful.
claims.argument: Write-ups of the Nuts 'N More pitch (Season 4, 2013) say Herjavec offered $250,000 for 50%. Cuban offered $75,000 upfront plus $175,000 for future orders, for 35%. The two sharks ended up with 35% together. No retrieved source gives a transcript with a shark warning that 50% would cause resentment at "16% each". The arithmetic is also unclear: 50% split between two sharks is 25% each, not 16%. The quote may come from a different segment or a loose paraphrase, so it can be neither confirmed nor refuted.
claims.summary: No source confirms which shark said this or the "16% each" detail.

claims.text: The Nuts and More founders asked the sharks to come down from 50% to about 30% with the tiered investment approach.
claims.argument: The speaker's own quote has the founders saying "50% is too much" and asking for "maybe 30% with that tiered approach." Write-ups of the episode agree that the founders countered at 30% and that the deal was staged, with $75,000 upfront and the rest for future purchase orders. The sharks held at 35% and ended with a 35% deal. The 50% opening offer is not stated in the retrieved articles, but the transcript supports it.
claims.summary: The 50% starting offer is not confirmed by the articles found.

claims.text: Robert and Mark agreed to a deal with the Nuts and More founders at 35% for the $250,000 investment.
claims.argument: Shark Tank coverage says Mark Cuban and Robert Herjavec invested $250,000 in Nuts 'N More for 35% equity. The founders countered with 30%, Mark held firm at 35%, and Robert agreed to join at that figure. That matches the transcript. The sources are mostly blogs and content sites, but they agree on the terms. One source says part of the money was paid upfront, which does not change the 35% for $250,000.
claims.summary: Mark Cuban and Robert Herjavec did invest $250,000 for 35% of Nuts 'N More.

claims.text: Darien Craig and Brandon Eckles are seeking $500,000 in exchange for 5% of their company, Y'all Sweet Tea.
claims.argument: Multiple outlets report that Darien Craig and Brandon Echols of Hayden, Alabama, pitched Y'all Sweet Tea on Shark Tank Season 16, Episode 5. They asked for $500,000 for 5% equity, a $10 million valuation. They later took a $500,000 for 15% deal from Lori Greiner and Rashaun Williams. "Eckles" is a transcript misspelling of "Echols", which doesn't change the substance.
claims.summary: The founders did ask for $500,000 for 5% of Y'all Sweet Tea on Shark Tank.

claims.text: Darien Craig and Brandon Eckles are from the town of Hayden, Alabama, and have known each other since they were 6 years old.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: Y'all Sweet Tea was launched in 2021.
claims.argument: Most outlets, including Starter Story and CNBC-syndicated coverage, date the company to 2021, when Darien Craig started it with $300 from his last paycheck. Mashed says it officially launched in 2021. A couple of sites (Shark Tank Talks, Cinemaholic) give 2015, apparently counting an earlier start. The claim is about the launch, and 2021 matches the launch date.
claims.summary: Y'all Sweet Tea launched in 2021, as the founders say, though a few sites give 2015.

claims.text: Other tea brands were not properly utilizing social media and influencers.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: One of Y'all Sweet Tea's top influencers, Mama Sue, has over 1 million followers.
claims.argument: Mama Sue (Sue Garrett, Harpersville, Alabama) is a real Southern grandmother-influencer who works with Y'all Sweet Tea. Shark Tank recap sites repeat the "over 1 million followers" line, but they take it from the on-air pitch. Independent profiles give older or vaguer numbers: Alabama Living reported 800,000+ Facebook followers, and another profile said "hundreds of thousands" of followers. Across her Facebook pages and YouTube, the total could plausibly pass 1 million, but no source confirms this.
claims.summary: Mama Sue is real and linked to the brand, but no source clearly shows over 1 million followers.

claims.text: Y'all Sweet Tea's influencers are southern grandmas.
claims.argument: The claim is the founders' own pitch line on Shark Tank Season 16, Episode 5. Coverage describes their influencer strategy as centered on Southern grandmothers, including Mama Sue (over 1 million followers) and Brenda Gantt. It is a self-description in a pitch, and not every influencer was individually verified, but it matches the company's stated strategy.
claims.summary: The founders said on Shark Tank that their influencers are Southern grandmas, and coverage matches this.

claims.text: Each bag of Y'all Sweet Tea contains 10 filter packs, each of which makes one gallon of tea, and the customer adds their own sweetener.
claims.argument: Multiple retailer listings describe Y'all Sweet Tea as 10 bags per pack, each making one gallon. The tea is sold unsweetened, so buyers add their own sweetener, as the founder said. The company's own site was not retrieved, but the retailer listings agree with each other.
claims.summary: Each pack has 10 gallon-size tea bags, unsweetened, so buyers add their own sugar.

claims.text: A package of Y'all Sweet Tea costs about $2.67 to make and is wholesaled for $4.34.
claims.argument: Several outlets covering the Shark Tank pitch report the same figures: $2.67 to make, $4.34 wholesale and $7.25 retail on the website. Shark Tank Blog derives wholesale and retail margins from these numbers. Food Republic gives rounder figures (about $2.50 and $4), which fits rounding. These are the founders' own pitch figures, which the claim attributes to them.
claims.summary: The founders did say a package costs $2.67 to make and sells wholesale for $4.34.

claims.text: Y'all Sweet Tea is 3 years in and has passed $10.3 million in sales since 2021.
claims.argument: Several outlets covering the Shark Tank episode (aired November 15, 2024) report the founders, Darien Craig and Brandon Echols, saying they had passed $10.3 million in sales since 2021, in about three years. The yearly figures given ($1.2M in 2021, $2M in 2022, $4M in 2023, and about $3M by October 2024) add up to roughly $10.2M, which is consistent with the total. The figure is the founders' own unaudited statement, and no independent financial filing was found. The "3 years in" framing matches the 2021–2024 span.
claims.summary: The founders said on Shark Tank they had passed $10.3 million in sales since 2021, and the yearly figures roughly fit.

claims.text: Y'all Sweet Tea's sales were $1.2 million in 2021, $2 million in 2022, and $4 million in 2023 (doubled).
claims.argument: Shark Tank Blog reports that Y'all Sweet Tea had $1.2 million in sales in its first year, doubled to $2 million the next, and reached $4 million in the third year. CNBC Make It (via NBC affiliates) also reports about $4 million in revenue for the latest full year. The $10.3 million cumulative total is consistent with these figures (1.2+2+4 is about 7.2 million through 2023, plus 2024 sales). All figures are founder-reported rather than audited, and the "first year" is described loosely as 2021.
claims.summary: The founders' sales figures of $1.2M, $2M and $4M match what other reports say.

claims.text: This year, Y'all Sweet Tea is at $3 million in sales year to date and projects to do $5 million plus for the year.
claims.argument: Coverage of the Shark Tank Season 16 Episode 5 pitch (aired Nov 15, 2024) says the founders reported about $3 million in sales so far that year and expected to finish above $5 million. The surrounding figures match: $1.2M in 2021, $2M in 2022, $4M in 2023, and $10.3M since 2021. "This year" means 2024, the year of the pitch, not 2026, when the clip was re-uploaded. These are the founders' own pitch claims, reported by entertainment and fan blogs rather than audited, and one source muddles whether the $5M target was for 2024 or 2025.
claims.summary: Only the founders' own pitch numbers back this, and no independent audit of the sales was found.

claims.text: Last year Y'all Sweet Tea profited 20%, almost $800,000, and this year it is pretty much break even after doubling down on Facebook ads, which it had never run before.
claims.argument: Coverage of the Shark Tank pitch (aired Nov. 15, 2024) reports $4 million in sales last year with a 20% profit margin. That matches roughly $800,000 in profit. Retrieved snippets did not mention the "pretty much break even" this year or the first-ever Facebook ads. These are the founders' own statements in the pitch, and no source contradicts them. The video was uploaded in 2026, but the statement comes from the 2024 pitch.
claims.summary: The 20% profit on $4 million fits, but break-even and Facebook ads were not confirmed.

claims.text: 85% of Y'all Sweet Tea's sales come directly through its website.
claims.argument: Coverage of the Shark Tank Season 16 pitch quotes co-founder Brandon Echols saying 85% of sales are direct-to-consumer. Another outlet says 85% come from the website, with the rest from Amazon and about 600 stores. The figure is a company-reported number from the 2024 pitch, not independently audited, and the channel mix may have shifted since (for example, Walmart shelf space). The claim matches what was said in the pitch.
claims.summary: The founder said on Shark Tank that 85% of sales were direct-to-consumer, mainly through the website.

claims.text: Y'all Sweet Tea is in about 600 grocery stores, mainly throughout the southeast.
claims.argument: Several outlets covering the Shark Tank pitch (season 16, aired November 2024) report that the founders said they were in about 600 grocery stores, mainly in the Southeast, and wanted big-box retail. Regional chains such as Piggly Wiggly, Foodland and Food City carry the tea, which fits the Southeast focus. A BevNet piece from 2024 says nearly 1,000 stores, so the count was growing or differs by source. The 600 figure is the founders' own pitch-time number and is consistent with a later article saying "over 600 stores" at the time of the pitch.
claims.summary: The exact current store count is not confirmed, and one report cites almost 1,000.

claims.text: Walmart talked to Y'all Sweet Tea a few months ago about doing a 500-store test.
claims.argument: The segment is from the Shark Tank Season 16 pitch (aired November 2024). Coverage of that pitch says the founders, Darien Craig and Brandon Echols, were in about 600 grocery stores, mostly in the Southeast, and had held early talks with Walmart about a 500-store test. No independent source confirms that Walmart made the offer. The claim therefore rests on the founders' own statement, and nothing contradicts it. "A few months ago" refers to the time of the pitch, not to the 2026 upload date.
claims.summary: Only the founders' own on-air statement supports the Walmart 500-store test talks.

claims.text: Y'all Sweet Tea has raised no money: no investors and no loans.
claims.argument: Shark Tank coverage of the Season 16 pitch (aired Nov 2024) says founders Darien Craig and Brandon Echols own 100% of Y'all Sweet Tea with no investors or loans, and the Sharks praised this. Other sources say the company is self-funded and shows no earlier funding rounds. A "Y'all Company" with a Honeycomb Credit debt round appeared in the results, but nothing links it to the tea brand. The claim rests on the founders' own statement plus secondary reporting, not on a financial filing.
claims.summary: The founders pitched owning 100% of the company, with no investors or loans, as they said.

claims.text: Y'all Sweet Tea had never done flavors before last year; it sold only regular tea until the flavored teas launched.
claims.argument: BevNET reported in 2024 that Y'all Sweet Tea was getting set to launch seven brand-new flavors, such as Raspberry, Watermelon and Half Tea-Half Lemonade. That fits the speaker's account that flavors were new and came after a regular-tea-only lineup. No source directly confirms that the brand sold only regular tea before. The phrase "last year" depends on the pitch's filming date (the Shark Tank episode aired in November 2024), so that detail is not pinned down.
claims.summary: No source states that the brand sold only regular tea before its first flavors.

claims.text: Y'all Sweet Tea launched flavored teas last year, and when it launched the peach bag it sold 10,000 of those bags in 35 minutes on its website.
claims.argument: Several outlets covering the Shark Tank pitch report that the Georgia Peach flavor, the company's first flavored tea, sold 10,000 units in 35 minutes. They also report $100,000 in the first eight minutes. The launch was in 2023, and the pitch aired in November 2024, so "last year" is right from the pitch's point of view, though not from the 2026 upload date. One source says 30 minutes instead of 35. The figures come from the founders themselves and could not be checked against sales records.
claims.summary: Y'all Sweet Tea's peach launch did sell 10,000 bags in about 35 minutes, as the founders said on Shark Tank.

claims.text: The first 8 minutes of the peach tea bag launch on Y'all Sweet Tea's website produced $100,000 in sales.
claims.argument: Several outlets covering Y'all Sweet Tea's Shark Tank appearance report that the Georgia Peach flavor sold 10,000 bags in about 35 minutes. They also report about $100,000 in sales in the first 8 minutes. Mashed attributes the sales to the brand's website. One outlet gives 30 minutes rather than 35 for the full sell-out, but the 8-minute, $100,000 figure is the same everywhere. The figures come from the founders' own statements and were not checked independently.
claims.summary: Several reports repeat that the peach launch made $100,000 in its first 8 minutes.

claims.text: Y'all Sweet Tea's founders believe the peach tea launch day could have been a million dollar day on their website.
claims.argument: No fact check available — this is a prediction about the future, which no source can confirm yet.

claims.text: A Shark offered $500,000 for 10% of Y'all Sweet Tea.
claims.argument: Search results say Rashaun Williams made the first offer of $500,000 for 10% of Y'all Sweet Tea on Shark Tank season 16, episode 5 (November 2024). The founders ultimately took a joint Greiner-Williams offer of $500,000 for 15%, but the 10% offer was made. The speaker's words ("I'll give you 500K for 10%") match this.
claims.summary: A Shark did offer $500,000 for 10% of Y'all Sweet Tea on the show.

claims.text: Y'all Sweet Tea's founders envision reaching $10 million to $20 million in sales and then eventually having an exit.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: Very few companies that walk into the Shark Tank have social media nailed the way Y'all Sweet Tea does.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: A Shark said you can't do Walmart without a distributor, but once one is set up you can also do other retailers like Target and Costco.
claims.argument: The claim only reports what a Shark said on the Season 16, Episode 5 pitch (aired Nov 15, 2024). The speaker's quoted passage matches it. Episode coverage says a distributor is needed to get into big chains like Walmart, Target and Costco. The Shark was Kevin O'Leary, who teamed with Rashaun Williams, and the claim leaves him unnamed as "A Shark". No verbatim transcript was retrieved, but nothing contradicts the paraphrase.
claims.summary: A Shark did say a distributor is needed for Walmart, and that it then opens the door to Target and Costco.

claims.text: Kevin offered 20% of Y'all Sweet Tea for $500,000, with 10% going to him and 10% to Rashan.
claims.argument: Several outlets report that Kevin O'Leary teamed with guest Shark Rashaun Williams and offered $500,000 for 20% equity, split evenly between them. This matches the transcript, "give us 20% for the 500, I get 10, he gets 10." One outlet (NNPA) says his offer was 15% from the start, but the more common account, and the transcript itself, says 20%. The final deal was with Lori and Rashaun at 15%, which is a separate matter.
claims.summary: Kevin did offer $500,000 for 20%, split 10% each with Rashan, as said.

claims.text: Lori offered to split the $500K with Rashan for 15% of the company.
claims.argument: Search results on Shark Tank Season 16, Episode 5 say Lori Greiner teamed with Rashaun Williams to offer $500,000 for 15% of Y'all Sweet Tea, a 7.5% stake each. The founders accepted this offer. This matches the claim that Lori would split the $500K with Rashaun for 15%.
claims.summary: Lori and Rashaun offered $500K together for 15% of the company, as said.

claims.text: Lori said she has tons of products that have done extremely well in grocery.
claims.argument: The quoted transcript has Lori saying "I have tons of products that have done extremely well in grocery." That is how she pitched her joint offer with Rashaun Williams on Y'all Sweet Tea (Season 16, Episode 5). Search summaries describe the same argument, citing her "tons of grocery" experience. Her portfolio includes grocery-sold items such as Bantam Bagels, which T. Marzetti acquired. The claim is only that she said this, so her actual grocery record is not in question.
claims.summary: Lori did say she has many products that have done very well in grocery stores.

claims.text: No one has been disruptive in the tea business for years.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: Lori offered Brandon and Darien $500K by herself for 10%, and said she would go in with Rashan for 20%.
claims.argument: Recaps of Shark Tank S16E5 say Rashaun Williams offered $500K for 10% on his own. Lori Greiner then joined him for a combined 15%, split 7.5% each. The 20% team-up with Rashaun came from Kevin O'Leary, who later dropped to 15%. The quoted lines in the transcript most likely belong to Kevin, so attributing them to Lori is wrong. Recaps vary on some details, such as who opened at 10%, which limits confidence.
claims.summary: Lori only offered with Rashaun for 15%. The solo 10% and the 20% team-up came from others, apparently Kevin.

claims.text: Brandon and Darien countered by asking for $750,000 for 15%.
claims.argument: A Shark Tank recap says the founders, Darien and Brandon, countered the Sharks' offers with $750K for 15%. The speaker's transcript matches this: "could we also raise some more cash to 750... So 750,000 for 15%." Other sources agree the final deal was $500K for 15% with Lori Greiner and Rashaun Williams. Few outlets mention the counter itself, so confidence is somewhat lower.
claims.summary: The founders did counter by asking for $750,000 for 15%, and then took a $500,000 deal instead.

claims.text: If the founders take $500K and later raise another round after succeeding, at 2 or 3x valuation they won't notice the difference in the equity they give up now, and the math works in their favor.
claims.argument: This is a negotiating opinion that holds in general: raising less now and more later at a higher valuation usually dilutes founders less in total. Worked examples (Burkland, CodingVC) show smaller total dilution for staged raises, and a modest difference after post-money effects. But the claim is stated categorically. It only works if the company hits milestones and later valuations rise (the "2 or 3x" assumption), and SVB notes the risk if valuation falls. Nobody ran the numbers for this exact $500K vs $750K deal, so "works in your favor" is plausible rather than proven.
claims.summary: Taking less now can cost less ownership overall, but only if the company grows and later valuations are higher.

claims.text: Brandon and Darien declined Mr. Wonderful's offer and accepted Lori and Rashan's offer of $200,000 for 15%.
claims.argument: Brandon Echols and Darien Craig of Y'all Sweet Tea turned down Kevin O'Leary (Mr. Wonderful) and took the joint offer from Lori Greiner and Rashaun Williams. Reports put that deal at $500,000 for 15%, not $200,000. The $200,000 figure comes from a different pitch (Laabox) that follows in the transcript. The core choice is right, but the amount is wrong.
claims.summary: They did pick Lori and Rashaun over Mr. Wonderful, but the deal was $500,000 for 15%, not $200,000.

claims.text: Lori and Rashan offered $200,000 for 15% of Laabox Portable Campfires.
claims.argument: The transcript shows the "Lori and Rashan's offer $200,000 for 15%" line was said while Mr. Wonderful declined the Y'all Sweet Tea pitch. Laabox's pitch (spelled LavaBox in sources) only begins right afterward, with Josh Thurmond asking $200,000 for 10%. In LavaBox's episode, sources report that Lori Greiner settled at 12.5% plus a royalty and Kevin O'Leary offered 10%. None mention Rashan or a 15% stake, and the deal never closed.
claims.summary: The $200,000 for 15% offer was for Y'all Sweet Tea; the campfire company got a 12.5% offer from Lori.

claims.text: Josh Thurman of Laabox Portable Campfires is seeking $200,000 for 10% equity in his company.
claims.argument: Multiple sources report that Josh Thurmond pitched LavaBox portable campfires on Shark Tank Season 14, asking $200,000 for 10% equity. The names are spelled "Laabox" and "Thurman" in the transcript; sources spell them "LavaBox" and "Thurmond". This is a transcription difference, not a factual error.
claims.summary: He did ask for $200,000 for 10%; only the name spellings (Lavabox, Thurmond) differ.

claims.text: Devastation created by human-caused wildfires is often totally preventable.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: The Lava Box starts with a military style ammo can and uses propane.
claims.argument: Seller and retailer pages describe the LavaBox as a portable propane fire pit built in a military-style (50 cal) ammo can. It uses a propane burner with regulator and hose, plus ceramic "Hades Stones". This matches the pitch on Shark Tank.
claims.summary: The Lava Box is a propane fire pit built inside a military-style ammo can.

claims.text: The Lava Box is the lightest product on the market right now with the biggest fire.
claims.argument: This is a sales boast made in a pitch. Searches found LavaBox's own pages calling its units compact and lightweight, but no weights or BTU figures. Nothing compared them with rivals such as the Outland Firecube (about 22 lb, 58,000 BTU in one guide). No independent source confirms or refutes "lightest on the market with the biggest fire".
claims.summary: No source confirms that the Lava Box is the lightest portable fire pit with the biggest fire.

claims.text: The Lava Box comes in three sizes: small, medium and large.
claims.argument: Secondary coverage of LavaBox's Shark Tank pitch says the product comes in three sizes, small, medium and large, with the small one the best seller. This matches the speaker's description. The company's own site lists "three sizes" mainly in terms of propane tank capacity, so the company-side confirmation is indirect. No source contradicts the claim.

claims.text: Pho is a Vietnamese rice noodle soup.
claims.argument: Pho is a noodle soup from northern Vietnam, dated to around 1900–1907. It is made of broth, flat rice noodles, herbs and beef or chicken. Encyclopedia and recipe sources agree on this description.
claims.summary: Pho is a Vietnamese soup made with broth and rice noodles.

claims.text: Traditionally, pho broth is made with fresh beef bones mixed with a variety of aromatic spices, simmered for hours.
claims.argument: Recipe and food-writing sources agree that traditional pho broth is made from beef bones (marrow, knuckle) simmered gently with aromatics such as star anise, cinnamon, cloves, coriander, and charred onion and ginger. Simmer times vary by recipe, from about 2 to 12 hours or more, and most traditional versions run several hours. The word "fresh" is a simplification, since bones are usually blanched first, but this is immaterial.
claims.summary: Pho broth is traditionally made by simmering beef bones with spices for hours.

claims.text: Felicious instant pho takes only five minutes to prepare.

claims.text: Felicious is made from a family formula developed from the founder's mom's secret recipe.

A retailer listing says the pho has a "special blend of aromatic whole spices in a tea bag form", which matches the claim. claims.text: Scrub Daddy's total sales on QVC were just north of $100,000 in only 4 months.
