claims.summary: In the pitch, the inventor said one sponge costs about a dollar to make.

claims.text: Scrub Daddy is sold wholesale for about $2.80.
claims.argument: Search results from transcripts of the Shark Tank pitch show the exchange. Krause says the cost to make one is about $1, and he sells it for about $2.80. The price is confirmed as wholesale. The claim matches what was said in the pitch. The sources are subtitle files and secondary summaries rather than an official transcript, and the wording around "Wholesale?" in the video is a little ambiguous, so confidence is moderate.
claims.summary: The $2.80 wholesale figure was seen only in subtitle transcripts and search summaries, not an official transcript.

claims.text: A Brillo pad, a traditional product, has a 20% margin.
claims.argument: The 20% figure is a shark's offhand estimate in the pitch, phrased as a question ("what is, a 20%"). Searches found no published margin for Brillo pads. Only shelf prices turned up, such as a 10-count pack at about $2.77 at Walmart. The Scrub Daddy pitch sources discuss a 20% equity stake, not a Brillo margin. The claim can be neither confirmed nor refuted.
claims.summary: No source gives Brillo's profit margin, so the 20% figure could not be checked.

claims.text: A company whose sales are completely dependent on QVC is a disaster waiting to happen.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

tags.name: Personal opinion
tags.definition: An evaluation a viewer hears as the speaker's own view; a note, not a technique.

evidence.text: when a company's sales are completely dependent on QVC, that's a disaster waiting to happen.

tags.explanation: The evaluation "that's a disaster waiting to happen" sounds like the speaker's own view about dependence on QVC.

claims.text: The Scrub Daddy founder says he has 3,000 stores lined up and will be in 3,000 stores.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: Scrub Daddy's maker also has other products: Scrub Mommy, Scrub Baby for baby bottles, and a sink holder with drains in the legs.
claims.argument: Scrub Daddy's own site sells Scrub Mommy, a Scrub Babies pack for baby bottles, and the Daddy Caddy sink holder, which is open so the sponge can drain. The exact "drains in the legs" design was not verified, but it fits the described holder. The speaker was describing products in the pitch; the maker does offer these lines today.
claims.summary: Scrub Daddy's maker does sell Scrub Mommy, Scrub Baby for baby bottles, and a sink holder (Daddy Caddy).

claims.text: QVC does over 8 billion dollars in sales a year.
claims.argument: QVC Group reported total 2024 revenue of $10,037 million, and its US segment (QxH) alone had $6,598 million. QVC, Inc. trailing twelve-month revenue was reported at about $8.53 billion as of May 2026, per an aggregator. Whichever QVC measure is used, sales are "over 8 billion" a year, though the figure has been declining and the US-only figure is below 8 billion.
claims.summary: QVC's yearly sales are well over 8 billion dollars, so the claim holds.

claims.text: Lori has personally done over 500 million dollars in sales on QVC.
claims.argument: The line comes from Greiner herself on Shark Tank, so it is her own self-reported figure. In an interview she put her retail sales near $500 million, but that covered QVC plus other retailers. One secondary source says about $350 million by 2010. No QVC or independent source gives a QVC-only lifetime total, so the claim is plausible but unverified.
claims.summary: Lori said it herself, but no independent source confirms $500 million in QVC-only sales.

claims.text: QVC rotates products in and out, and once products are out of QVC they are out.
claims.argument: QVC confirmed it has an "ever changing portfolio of products" when it quietly dropped MyPillow, so the rotation part holds. The absolute "once out, they're out" is Cuban's negotiating rhetoric. No source establishes that removal is permanent, and Scrub Daddy itself was featured on QVC repeatedly. The claim is partly supported and overstated.
claims.summary: No source shows that products dropped from QVC are permanently gone.

claims.text: One shark offers $50,000 for 15% of Scrub Daddy, if the founder can raise the rest from Lori.
claims.argument: Summaries of the Scrub Daddy Shark Tank episode say Daymond John, seeing a partnership with Lori Greiner, proposed $50,000 for 15% contingent on Greiner joining him. This matches the claim's offer and its condition. Greiner is also widely called the "Queen of QVC". The sources are secondary and the full transcript wasn't opened, so some uncertainty remains.
claims.summary: Only secondary summaries mention the $50,000 for 15% offer, and no full transcript was checked.

claims.text: One shark offers $100,000 for 30% and says he would get Scrub Daddy into an infomercial right away and into all retail stores across the country within literally weeks.
claims.argument: Episode summaries of the Scrub Daddy pitch (Season 4, Episode 7) describe a Shark, named as Lori Greiner, opening with $100,000 for 30%. She also promised an immediate infomercial and nationwide retail placement within weeks. The final deal was $200,000 for 20%, which does not contradict an earlier, lower offer. No full transcript was retrieved, so the exact wording rests on summaries and the speaker's own quote. The claim only says "one shark", so it holds either way.
claims.summary: The exact "within literally weeks" wording and which Shark said it were not verified in a full transcript.

claims.text: One shark offers $100,000 in exchange for 50 cents on every unit sold until the $100K is recouped, then 10 cents per unit in perpetuity, with the founder keeping the whole company.
claims.argument: The video's own quoted transcript matches the claim. The shark offers $100,000 and says "You're going to keep the whole company". He asks for 50 cents per unit until the $100K is back, then 10 cents in perpetuity. A recap of the Scrub Daddy pitch says O'Leary's offer was "$100,000 for 50 cents on each unit sold until he recoups his investment and later 10 cents per unit, which would last forever." Other recaps give different later figures (7.5 cents), but the 50-then-10 version agrees with the transcript.
claims.summary: Kevin O'Leary did offer $100,000 for 50 cents a unit, then 10 cents, with no equity taken.

claims.text: A 50 cents per unit royalty would increase the company's cost of goods sold by 50%.
claims.argument: In the pitch, Aaron Krause says it costs about $1 to make one Scrub Daddy, and he sells it wholesale for about $2.80. O'Leary's offer was a royalty of 50 cents per unit until he recouped his $100,000, then 10 cents per unit. Against a $1 unit cost, 50 cents is a 50% increase in cost of goods sold. The speaker's remark is slightly loose, because the royalty drops to 10 cents after recoup, but the 50% figure holds for the initial period.
claims.summary: Each sponge cost about $1 to make, so a 50-cent royalty adds about 50% to that cost.

claims.text: Lori offered $100,000 for 25% of the company, saying she is partnered with the best of them and that a QVC infomercial could get the product into every retailer worldwide.
claims.argument: Sources agree that Lori Greiner won Scrub Daddy with $200,000 for 20%, after a bidding war in which she, Daymond John and Kevin O'Leary competed. Her QVC connection was central to her pitch. None of the retrieved pages gives the episode's line-by-line dialogue. They do not show whether the "$100,000 for 25%" revision, the "partnered with the best of them" line and the QVC infomercial pitch came from Lori or from another Shark. The claim is plausible but could not be checked.
claims.summary: No source shows who made the $100,000 for 25% offer; Lori's final deal was $200,000 for 20%.

claims.text: The product may sell 10 million units.
claims.argument: No fact check available — this is a prediction about the future, which no source can confirm yet.

claims.text: Lori just did a half-billion-dollar deal with Walmart.
claims.argument: Searches found no report of a Lori Greiner and Walmart deal worth $500 million. Her Shark Tank products, including Scrub Daddy, are sold at Walmart, but no source gives a half-billion-dollar agreement. The line appears in a heated on-air exchange and may be hyperbole or refer to something unreported, so it can be neither confirmed nor refuted.
claims.summary: No source confirms a $500 million Walmart deal for Lori Greiner.

claims.text: The bidding escalated: Damon offered $150,000 for 25%, Kevin offered $100,000 for no equity plus 10 cents a unit, Lori went to $150,000 for 25%, then another shark went to $175,000, and then another to $200,000.
claims.argument: Secondary sources agree that Daymond John offered $150,000 for 25%. They also say Kevin O'Leary offered $100,000 as venture debt with a per-unit royalty ending at 10 cents. Lori Greiner won with $200,000 for 20%. No retrieved source or transcript confirms the middle steps, such as another shark at $175,000 and then another at $200,000, or their order. Nothing found contradicts the claim, but the sources are thin and mostly summaries.
claims.summary: The Damon, Kevin and Lori offers fit reports, but the $175,000 and $200,000 steps were not confirmed.

claims.text: Botit founders Maurice Bachelor and Joel Griffith said Botit is a website and mobile app that uses artificial intelligence to complete online tasks.
claims.argument: News coverage confirms that Maurice Bachelor and Joel Griffith pitched Bot-It, an AI automation website and app, on Shark Tank Season 15 in 2023, asking $150,000 for 10%. No retrieved page prints their opening line word for word. The speaker's text is the founders' own on-air pitch, so attribution is very likely right, but the wording could not be checked against a transcript.
claims.summary: The founders did pitch on Shark Tank, but the exact opening line was not found in text.

quote.author: Maurice Bachelor and Joel Griffith
quote.quoted_text: together we founded Botit, a website [music] and mobile app that uses artificial intelligence to complete online tasks.

claims.text: Online reservations, golf tee times and concert tickets are often gone within seconds because bots book them faster than humans can.
claims.argument: Reports show bots buy concert tickets at speeds humans cannot match. New York's attorney general described a bot buying over 1,000 U2 tickets in one minute. Restaurant reservation bots on Resy and OpenTable are also documented. Golf tee times were not specifically covered in the results. The claim says "often", which is a loose generalization, since high demand also makes tickets sell out.
claims.summary: Golf tee time bots were not specifically confirmed.

claims.text: Bots now control 50% of online traffic for things like booking reservations and making online purchases.
claims.argument: Imperva/Thales reports put bots at about 51% of all internet traffic in 2024 and 53% in 2025, so "about 50%" matches overall web traffic. The claim, however, ties the figure to booking reservations and online purchases. No source found gives 50% for that. Sector figures vary: airline traffic was about 44% bad bots and travel sites were reported near 59% bots. The headline number is roughly right but misapplied.
claims.summary: Bots are about half of all web traffic, but that isn't specifically booking and buying traffic.

claims.text: Botit's founders say it is almost impossible for humans to click as fast as a bot.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: Botit offers pre-built bots that users can select to start automating in seconds, or users can customize and Botit will build one for them.
claims.argument: Coverage of Bot-It says it has a slate of pre-built bots, such as tee times, concert tickets and dinner reservations. It also sells a custom-made, purpose-built bot option. The company FAQ describes picking a template and configuring it. "In seconds" is marketing wording that no source tests.
claims.summary: Bot-It really offers ready-made bots, and it also sells custom-built ones.

claims.text: Botit is an application that lets users go on any website and specify steps (click a button, log in, type information), and Botit's backend system then automates that process.
claims.argument: Multiple outlets describe Bot-It (Shark Tank Season 15) as a website and mobile app that uses automation to carry out online tasks such as restaurant, camping and tennis bookings. Users pick a website and set up the steps, and Bot-It then runs them. This matches the founders' own description on the show. The name is usually written "Bot-It", but that is a spelling nuance.
claims.summary: Bot-It is an app that automates online tasks like reservations by following steps users set up.

claims.text: Michael, a shark who works at Topps, says there are probably billions of dollars of products that bots try to buy from his companies each year.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: Bots come to buy everything when Topps makes a card release, and the same happens when a new Mitchell Ness jersey is released.
claims.argument: The claim comes from a Topps representative describing his own company's experience, so it is first-hand but unverified. Public petitions say bots buy out trading card releases within seconds, which fits the general pattern. No retrieved source specifically confirms bots targeting Topps releases or Mitchell & Ness jerseys, and none contradicts it.
claims.summary: Bot complaints about card releases exist, but no source confirms Topps or Mitchell & Ness bot attacks as described.

claims.text: Topps has built software to eliminate bots.
claims.argument: Topps' own FAQ says it partners with the third-party platform EQL for high-demand launches, which it says helps "slow down bots" and make launches fair. This shows Topps takes anti-bot steps, but it points to a bought-in tool rather than software Topps built. It also describes slowing bots, not eliminating them. EQL reports zero bot interference at the WrestleMania launch, but that is the vendor's own claim. The speaker may be loosely describing Topps' overall bot defenses, and no source rules out in-house tooling.
claims.summary: Topps does fight bots, but it uses an outside company's tool that slows bots down, not its own that removes them.

claims.text: Botit says it built its technology to be undetectable so that it can get on any website it needs to.
claims.argument: In the Shark Tank pitch quoted in the claim, Bot-It's co-founder says "we built our technology to now be able to be undetectable. So, we can get on any website that we need to." A recap of the Season 15 pitch also reports that Bachelor said Bot-It had been made undetectable, without explaining how. The claim reports what the company says. It does not assert that the technology really is undetectable, and no independent test of that was found.
claims.summary: The Bot-It founder did say on the show that its tech was built to be undetectable.

claims.text: Botit follows all standard practices for automation and does nothing outside of what is regulated.
claims.argument: The claim is the founder's own description of the company on Shark Tank. Coverage confirms that Bot-It says it is undetectable and can get on any website. It also confirms that Michael Rubin of Fanatics complained about bots. No source audits Bot-It's practices or finds that it broke a law. General sources say bot use usually breaks retailer terms of service, and that getting around detection is the riskier area. That makes "nothing outside what is regulated" questionable, but it does not disprove it, so the claim can't be settled either way.
claims.summary: No source shows whether Bot-It really follows all automation rules; it only says it is undetectable.

claims.text: Botit has over $30,000 in sales, started 3 months ago, and has over 350 current subscribers.
claims.argument: Shark Tank fan and recap sites report that Bot-It told the Sharks it started about 3 months earlier, with about $30,000 in sales and 350 subscribers. This matches the claim, but these sites only repeat the pitch. No company filing, press report or other independent source verifies the figures, and one profile marks the $30k lifetime sales figure as "estimated". Nothing contradicts the claim, so it stays unverified.
claims.summary: The numbers match what the founders said on Shark Tank, but no independent source checks them.

claims.text: Botit signed up the largest shipping logistics company in Turkey as a B2B customer.
claims.argument: Coverage of Bot-It's Shark Tank appearance (Sportskeeda and similar write-ups) says the company had secured a partnership with Turkey's largest shipping and logistics company. That matches the speaker's wording. No source names the customer or gives independent proof such as a press release. The claim therefore rests on the founders' own statement, repeated by secondary outlets, and no source contradicts it.
claims.summary: The Turkish company is not named, so the "largest" label cannot be checked independently.

claims.text: A Botit subscription costs up to $40 for the standard package.
claims.argument: The claim repeats what the founder said in a Shark Tank pitch. Third-party recap sites list Standard at $9.99 a month and Standard Plus at $25 a month, with Pro at about $99.99 and Pro Plus at $275 a year. One article gives a range of $40 for standard packages up to $300 for professional-level access, which matches the founder's words. That article is described as conflicting with the others and possibly unreliable. No official pricing page was found. "Up to $40" is vague and fits neither confirmed nor refuted.
claims.summary: Bot-It's prices are reported inconsistently, so the "up to $40" standard price can't be confirmed.

claims.text: Botit's founder says he has spent over the last 15 years starting and scaling businesses and helped start the mobile division at Legal Zoom.
claims.argument: Maurice Bachelor is Bot-It's founder and CEO. Profiles and company databases list LegalZoom in his work history. A VC Post profile says he took over LegalZoom's mobile division in August 2018 and helped build its mobile-first experience. That profile reads like promotional material, so it is treated with caution. "Helped start" is slightly looser than "took over", and the "15 years" figure is his own estimate that sources could not verify. Nothing found contradicts the claim.
claims.summary: The exact "15 years" and "helped start" wording could not be checked against a firm source.

claims.text: One Botit founder is originally from Trenton, New Jersey, graduated from Morris College, and spent 10 years working in social media advertising for companies including LinkedIn, Snapchat, Amazon advertising and most recently TikTok.
claims.argument: Bot-It co-founder Joel Griffith is described as from Trenton, New Jersey, with about 10 years in social media advertising. Another article lists LinkedIn, Snap, Amazon and TikTok among his employers. A Morehouse News headline names "Joel Griffith '09" as Bot-It's head of growth, so the "Morris College" in the claim is probably a transcription of "Morehouse College". I did not open the Morehouse page itself, so this match rests on the headline alone.
claims.summary: Co-founder Joel Griffith is from Trenton with a 10-year social media ad career; the college is likely Morehouse.

claims.text: The use of bots in buying products is becoming a moral issue in society today.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: Fanatics is trying to eliminate bots, and is fighting to stop B2B bots so that products go to actual consumers.
claims.argument: The claim is Michael Rubin's own statement of intent. It matches what sources show about Fanatics. Fanatics describes a proprietary anti-bot mitigation and randomization system for its card drops. Its terms let it cancel orders and close accounts of people buying for resale. Coverage of Rubin's Shark Tank bid for Bot-It also says Fanatics was flooded with bot orders on limited collectibles and built anti-bot software. No source specifically addresses "B2B bots", and the claim is self-reported, so some doubt remains.
claims.summary: No source specifically confirms Fanatics' fight against business-run bots beyond the executive's own words.

claims.text: Botit does not help people get into their favorite restaurant on a given night; it helps when something opens up at a specific time, such as online reservations for a new restaurant or tea times released at 8 a.m. on Tuesday.
claims.argument: Bot-It is an automation service for tee times and dinner reservations, and booking slots as they open fits its purpose. However, the company also advertises a cancellation bot that runs every few minutes to pick up cancelled reservations, a self-reported 85% success rate on most golf courses. That means it may help in the "favorite restaurant tonight" scenario, which the speaker says it does not. Sources do not detail release-timing mechanics or restaurant-specific performance, so the speaker's description is partly right and partly oversimplified.
claims.summary: Bot-It does book slots the moment they open, but it also claims to snatch cancellations, so it may help with full restaurants.

claims.text: With all the new AI stuff coming out, people will become more aware of and more interested in using bots like Botit's if the right user interface is created.
claims.argument: No fact check available — this is a prediction about the future, which no source can confirm yet.

claims.text: One shark offered $150K for 20% of the Botit company.
claims.argument: Coverage of the Season 15 Shark Tank episode says the founders asked for $150,000 for 10% of Bot-It. Mark Cuban answered with $150,000 for 20%, and the video quotes this offer. Michael Rubin then competed with his own offer. The final deal reported was $300,000 for 30% from both sharks, which does not change the fact that one shark made this offer.
claims.summary: Mark Cuban offered $150,000 for 20% of Bot-It, as the speaker says.

claims.text: A second shark countered with an offer of $150K for 15% of Botit.
claims.argument: Coverage of Shark Tank Season 15, Episode 3 says one shark offered $150,000 for 20% and the other shark undercut it with $150,000 for 15%. This matches the quoted exchange, where the second shark says "I'll do 150 for 15% then." A few outlets misprint the figure as $50,000, but most sources give $150,000. The sharks later joined for $300K for 30%.
claims.summary: After an offer of $150K for 20%, another shark did offer $150K for 15% of Bot-It.

claims.text: One shark said he is highly regulated in every financial market he works in, and that regulators do not all agree that using bots is fair play.
claims.argument: The transcript quotes a shark saying: "I look at it from the moral issue and I'm highly regulated in every financial market I work in. They don't all agree with the idea that it's fair ball. I'm out." The claim paraphrases this accurately. Coverage of Bot-It on Season 15, Episode 3 says Kevin O'Leary dropped out because he disagreed with bots on moral grounds, which fits. None of the retrieved coverage quotes the regulation line verbatim, so the wording rests on the transcript itself.
claims.summary: A shark did say this when he dropped out of the Bot-It pitch, on moral grounds.

claims.text: Mark Cuban said that he would rather disrupt himself than have someone else disrupt him.
claims.argument: Searches found no source with Cuban saying "I'd rather disrupt myself than have someone else disrupt me." Coverage of the Bot-It episode (Season 15, 2023) does not print this line from anyone. In the clip, the line comes right before a remark addressed to the speaker ("I'd like to see you kick Cuban under the bus"), which suggests the speaker is not Cuban, probably Michael Rubin. Cuban has made similar points about self-disruption, but not in these words.
claims.summary: No record was found of Cuban saying these words; in the clip another shark seems to say them.

quote.author: Mark Cuban
quote.quoted_text: I rather disrupt myself than have someone else disrupt.

claims.text: In a clip, a Shark Tank investor, who appears to be Mark Cuban, tells Botit that he is not giving the sharks much because Botit asked $150,000 for 10% to get both of them (Cuban and Michael Rubin) in, since he likes Michael.
claims.argument: Recaps of Shark Tank Season 15 (2023) confirm that Bot-It asked $150,000 for 10%. Cuban offered 20% and Rubin offered 15%, and the founders asked them to partner. The final deal was $300,000 for 30%. No retrieved page gives the dialogue verbatim, so the speaker and the exact line could not be checked.
claims.summary: The episode is real, but no transcript confirms who said these exact words.

quote.author: Mark Cuban (apparent speaker in the clip)
quote.quoted_text: You're not giving us a whole lot cuz you asked 150 for 10 to get both of us in cuz I like Michael, right?

claims.text: Cuban and Rubin agreed to invest $300,000 for 30% of Botit in a joint deal with the Poochie brothers.
claims.argument: Multiple outlets report that on Shark Tank Season 15, Episode 3 (Oct 2023), Mark Cuban and Michael Rubin combined offers to invest $300,000 for 30% of Bot-It. The founders are named as Maurice Bachelor and Joel Griffith, and no retrieved source mentions "Poochie brothers" as partners in the deal. The deal terms are right, but the "Poochie brothers" detail is unsupported. Whether the deal closed after the show is disputed, which does not affect the on-air agreement.
claims.summary: Cuban and Rubin did offer $300,000 for 30% of Bot-It, but no source mentions "Poochie brothers".

claims.text: Christopher Gray from Philadelphia, Pennsylvania is seeking $40,000 for 15% of his company Scoly.
claims.argument: Reports on Shark Tank Season 6 (aired February 2015) say Christopher Gray, a Drexel student in Philadelphia, pitched his scholarship app asking $40,000 for 15%. Lori Greiner and Daymond John then offered the $40,000 for 15% between them. The company's name is spelled "Scholly", and "Scoly" is a transcript spelling error that does not change the substance.
claims.summary: He did ask for $40,000 for 15%; the app's real spelling is Scholly.

claims.text: The cost of college rises every year, forcing students and parents to take out student loans.
claims.argument: College Board data show published tuition rose by under 3% (nominal) for 2025-26, with a real increase under 1%. Net prices, what students actually pay after aid, have been flat or falling in real terms in some sectors, so "rises every year" is true mainly for sticker prices. Loans are common but not universal: about 36% of undergraduates borrow federal direct loans, and 44% of first-time full-time students received loan aid in 2017-18. The pitch is a loose generalization (a pitch opener), directionally reasonable but overstated.
claims.summary: Sticker prices do rise most years, but only a minority of students borrow, so "forced" overstates it.

claims.text: The cost of college rises every year.
claims.argument: The College Board's 2025 report shows published tuition and fees rose again for 2025-26: 2.7% at public two-year colleges and 4.0% at private nonprofit four-year colleges. That fits the speaker's general statement. Adjusted for inflation, sticker prices have fallen over a decade, and net prices (after grants) have declined at many institutions. So "rises every year" holds in nominal sticker terms but not for what students actually pay in real terms.
claims.summary: Sticker prices of college go up each year, though prices after aid and adjusted for inflation have often fallen.

claims.text: Students and parents are forced to take out student loans to pay for college, which puts many students in insurmountable debt.
claims.argument: US student debt is about $1.87 trillion across roughly 42-43 million federal borrowers, with an average federal balance near $39,600. As of March 2026, about 9.5 million federal borrowers (more than one in five) were in default, and New York Fed data show delinquency around 10-11% of balances. That supports the claim that many students end up in debt they cannot repay. "Forced" and "insurmountable" are rhetorical: not every student borrows and not every borrower is unable to repay. The core assertion holds as a general statement.
claims.summary: The share of students who borrow was not checked, so "forced" and "insurmountable" remain loose wording.

claims.text: Scholarships are extremely hard to find, causing millions of dollars in free scholarship money to go to waste because many students don't know it exists.
claims.argument: Surveys suggest many students find it hard to locate scholarships (e.g., 45% in a FluidReview survey, as retold secondhand). However, the claim that millions of dollars in scholarship money go to waste is a widely debunked myth. Mark Kantrowitz says more than $6 billion is awarded each year and almost none goes unclaimed. Some narrow-criteria awards go unused, and students do leave financial aid (e.g., Pell/FAFSA) on the table by not applying, so the point is partly right but overstated.
claims.summary: Finding scholarships is hard for many students, but scholarship money mostly doesn't go unused; that's a myth.

claims.text: Scoly is a mobile app, available for iPhone and Android, that matches students with hundreds of potential scholarships based on information such as their state and GPA, producing a list in minutes.
claims.argument: "Scoly" is the spoken form of Scholly, the scholarship-matching app from Christopher Gray, which appeared on Shark Tank in 2015. Sources describe students entering details such as home state, GPA and major and getting matched scholarships. Common Sense Media lists it for iPhone and Android. The exact "hundreds" of matches and the "minutes" timing are the pitch's own wording and were not independently checked, and the app's current pricing is unclear.
claims.summary: The app, spelled Scholly, exists on iPhone and Android and matches students to scholarships by state and GPA.

claims.text: Christopher Gray aggregated the scholarship list from different websites and manually input it into the Scoly database, after building a scholarship database and helping students for a couple of years.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: Christopher Gray has two co-founders, both app and web developers, and he is the CEO of Scoly.
claims.argument: No fact check available — claim is not independently verifiable.

claims.text: Christopher Gray is a junior undergraduate at Drexel University who won $1.3 million in scholarships, which took about 7 months at the beginning of his junior year to find.
claims.argument: Drexel and press coverage say Christopher Gray, a Drexel junior, won 34 scholarships worth $1.3 million out of 72 applications. Coverage also says the search took about seven months. This matches the claim and the company he founded, Scholly (spelled "Scoly" in the transcript). The "junior" status dates to about 2013, so it is not true of him in 2026. The video appears to be an older pitch re-uploaded, so the claim is judged as the clip's own time frame.
claims.summary: It is not confirmed that the pitch was filmed when he was a junior, rather than being an old clip.

claims.text: Christopher Gray received the Bill Gates scholarship, a full ride to any college you want to go to.
claims.argument: No retrieved source mentions a Christopher Gray winning The Gates Scholarship or $1.3 million in awards. The Gates Scholarship is real and covers the full cost of attendance left after other aid for four years. It is limited to accredited, nonprofit four-year US schools, so "any college you want" is a loose paraphrase. The personal claim cannot be verified from the searches.
claims.summary: No source confirms that Christopher Gray won the Gates Scholarship; the award itself is not valid at "any college."

claims.text: With Scoly, every student that uses the app is matched with between 120 and 220 scholarships totaling over $4 million.
claims.argument: The app is Scholly (spelled "Scoly" in the transcript). A Smithsonian article, as relayed in search results, says Scholly generates a list of 100 to 200 or more scholarships that can amount to as much as $4 million per user. The $4 million figure matches, but the count differs (120–220 versus 100–200+), and "as much as" is a ceiling, not a guaranteed total. A 2026 company figure was not found, so the speaker's range may be a newer update, but this is unconfirmed.
claims.summary: Scholly's older claim is 100–200+ scholarships worth up to $4 million, not exactly 120–220 for everyone.

claims.text: Scoly focuses on outside scholarships, not institutional scholarships.
claims.argument: Scholly (the app the speaker calls "Scoly") is described by a university scholarship listing as a free app to match students with external scholarships. A secondary source calls it a matching app that pairs students with outside scholarships, meaning awards not tied to a particular school. One third-party blog says its database also includes some university awards, and Scholly publishes no breakdown. So "focuses on outside scholarships" is a fair description, though not an exclusive rule.
claims.summary: Scholly does not publish how many of its awards are outside versus school-run.

claims.text: About $100 million in outside scholarships goes unclaimed, mainly because students don't know they exist.
claims.argument: The "about $100 million unclaimed" figure is widely repeated. It dates to 2005 NPR coverage and is attributed by SoFi to the National Scholarship Providers Association. No primary data backs it, and Mark Kantrowitz (Saving for College) argues that almost no scholarship money goes unclaimed. Sources say any unclaimed money usually reflects a lack of applicants or qualified applicants, which is only loosely the same as students not knowing the scholarships exist. The claim therefore states a contested estimate as settled fact.
claims.summary: The $100 million unclaimed figure is a common but unproven estimate that experts dispute.

claims.text: Scoly costs 99 cents in the app store.
claims.argument: The app is Scholly, pitched by Christopher Gray on Shark Tank in 2015. Coverage from that era (TechCrunch and others) says it was sold for $0.99 on iOS and Android, and the Sharks said that was too low. Later sources say the price rose or moved to a subscription, and the app is now free through Sallie Mae. So the 99-cent price matches the pitch-time statement but not the app's later pricing. The 92,000 paid-apps figure was not checked here.
claims.summary: Current App Store price could not be confirmed, and the 92,000 sales figure is unverified.

claims.text: Scoly has sold 92,000 paid apps in less than a year.
claims.argument: The app is Scholly, founded by Christopher Gray, who pitched it on Shark Tank (aired February 2015) when it cost 99 cents. A search summary of the Philadelphia Inquirer's coverage says the app had about 92,000 downloads at the time of the pitch, with no marketing budget. Because the app was paid at 99 cents, downloads are roughly paid sales. Technical.ly gave a lower figure of about 60,000 downloads, so the exact count varies by source. The "less than a year" timing was not independently confirmed. The pitch is also from 2015 and was re-uploaded in 2026, so the figure describes the app then, not now.
claims.summary: The 92,000 figure is only reported as downloads, and the "less than a year" timing is not confirmed.

claims.text: The Scoly app's sales came with zero marketing.
claims.argument: The speaker says the app's sales came with "zero marketing", yet in the same breath he describes an "effective PR strategy" of pitching reporters about his $1.3 million in scholarships. Press outreach is a form of marketing, so the claim holds at most for paid advertising. Coverage confirms the 99-cent app and that early downloads were about 40,000 after six months, but no source confirms 92,000 sales or the absence of marketing. The app was also later publicised through Shark Tank.
claims.summary: He did no paid ads, but he pitched reporters, which is marketing, so 'zero marketing' is overstated.

claims.text: Christopher Gray won $1.3 million in scholarships and used that fact to pitch reporters about the app he created for other people.
claims.argument: Multiple outlets (Smithsonian, Black Enterprise, Drexel) report that Christopher Gray won about $1.3 million in scholarships for college, and he then created the Scholly app. Press coverage of his story consistently centres on that figure, which fits his statement that he used it to pitch reporters. The pitching strategy itself rests on Gray's own words, and no independent source was found for it. The app's name is Scholly; "Scoly" is a transcription slip.
claims.summary: Gray did win about $1.3 million in scholarships and built the Scholly app; the pitching detail is his own account.

claims.text: Scoly's database contains between 10 and 20,000 scholarships.
claims.argument: "Scoly" is Scholly, the scholarship-matching app from Shark Tank. In context, "between 10 to 20,000" means 10,000 to 20,000 scholarships. A 2015 Fortune article reported 10,000 to 20,000 scholarships in the database at any given time, and TechCrunch cited "over 20,000". The count varies through the year, and no current figure from Scholly was found. The figure matches the 2015 coverage.
claims.summary: Only 2015-era reports give the size of the database, and the figure changes through the year.

claims.text: Scoly's co-founder developed an algorithm that gathered the scholarships from different sources.
claims.argument: The app is Scholly (the claim's "Scoly" is a misspelling). Black Enterprise reports that founder Christopher Gray manually listed scholarships from different websites, while the algorithm, built by his two other co-founders, handles the rest. So a co-founder did develop an algorithm, but the claim that it gathered scholarships from different sources is not what the sources say: the gathering was manual and the algorithm does matching. Other sources credit Gray or Pirollo differently, which adds some doubt.
claims.summary: Co-founders did build Scholly's matching algorithm, but founder Gray gathered the scholarships by hand.

claims.text: Damon and Lori offered to go in as 50/50 partners, $20,000 from her and $20,000 from him, for 15% of Scoly, and the founder accepted the deal.
claims.argument: The company is Scholly (the claim writes "Scoly"), and "Damon" is Daymond John. Founder Christopher Gray asked for $40,000 for 15%. Lori Greiner and John split it, $20,000 each for 15%, and Gray accepted. The sources are secondary retellings, but they agree with the transcript, and Robert Herjavec and Kevin O'Leary's objections on air also fit it.
claims.summary: Daymond John and Lori Greiner offered $20,000 each for 15% of Scholly, and the founder said yes.

claims.text: The founder of a previously funded app (apparently one Mark Cuban or another shark backed) sold it at 99 cents an app and it was downloaded 92,000 times.
claims.argument: The details match Scholly, the scholarship app pitched on Shark Tank in 2015. It sold for $0.99, and the 92,000 download figure was stated on the show. Founder Chris Gray got a $40,000 offer from Lori Greiner and Daymond John, which sparked a dispute among the Sharks. The company later said the 92,000 may have mixed up users and downloads, and other reports cite about 60,000 downloads. The "previously funded" wording in the claim is loose, since Scholly was pitching at the time, and no Shark is named as its backer.
claims.summary: No independent source confirms 92,000 actual downloads; only the on-air figure is reported.

claims.text: Dr. Adil Akar of San Diego, California is seeking $1 million for 2% equity in his company Psionic, which develops advanced bionic limbs accessible for both humans and robots.
claims.argument: The names "Adil Akar" and "Psionic" appear to be transcript misspellings of Dr. Aadeel Akhtar and PSYONIC. Reports say he pitched the Ability Hand on Shark Tank Season 15 (2024), asking $1 million for 2% equity at a $50 million valuation. PSYONIC is based in San Diego and makes bionic limbs for humans and robots (for example, a partnership with ABB Robotics). The pitch aired in 2024, though the video was uploaded in 2026.
claims.summary: The pitch is real: Dr. Aadeel Akhtar of San Diego asked $1 million for 2% of PSYONIC; names are caption misspellings.

claims.text: The ability hand is the fastest bionic hand on the market.
claims.argument: The Ability Hand's maker, PSYONIC, says it closes in about 200 ms and calls it the fastest bionic hand in the world. That is faster than the older estimates found for i-Limb (about 600 ms), Michelangelo (about 370 ms) and bebionic (800 ms or more). Those figures come from different methods. No independent head-to-head benchmark was found, and no source contradicts the claim.
claims.summary: No independent side-by-side test confirms it is the fastest bionic hand.

claims.text: The ability hand is the first bionic hand to provide touch feedback to users.
claims.argument: PSYONIC and outlets such as Fox News and Interesting Engineering describe the Ability Hand as the first touch-sensing bionic hand. Its sensors detect grip force and send vibration to the arm. Earlier research prostheses already gave sensory feedback: LifeHand 2 (Italy) and the Utah LUKE arm, which researchers say "isn't the first prosthetic to provide users with sensory feedback". The claim is defensible only as "first commercial" or "first of its kind on the market", and even that rests on company marketing. Stated flatly, it overstates.
claims.summary: Touch feedback in prosthetic hands existed before; "first" is a company marketing claim, not an established fact.

claims.text: The Psionic ability hand can be controlled with the user's muscles, is water resistant and is USB-C rechargeable.
claims.argument: Sources describing the PSYONIC Ability Hand list an IP64 rating, meaning it resists splashes and dust, though it should not be submerged. They say it charges over USB-C in about an hour. It works with EMG (muscle-signal) pattern recognition and direct-control systems, so the user's muscles can control it. "Water resistant" fits IP64 well.
claims.summary: The Ability Hand works with muscle signals, resists water splashes, and charges by USB-C.

claims.text: Sergeant Anderson can hold and feel his daughter's hand again with the ability hand, something he couldn't do with any other prosthetic before.
claims.argument: Sergeant Garrett Anderson, a veteran who lost his hand in Iraq, appeared with PSYONIC founder Aadeel Akhtar on Shark Tank. Secondary write-ups say he described feeling his daughter's hand through the Ability Hand's touch sensing. The "couldn't do with any other prosthetic" part is the pitch's own framing and could not be independently checked. It is plausible, since the hand is marketed as the first with touch feedback. Sources were mostly secondary or promotional.
claims.summary: The "never possible with any other prosthetic" part rests only on the company's and user's own accounts.

claims.text: The ability hand is being used on robots around the world, including at major tech companies and on missions into space.
claims.argument: Several sources list NASA, Meta, Google, Amazon and others as users of PSYONIC's Ability Hand in robotics, and it has been integrated on Apptronik's Apollo and NASA's Valkyrie. The "missions into space" part is looser: sources describe NASA preparing Valkyrie with the hand for a future space mission, and no primary NASA source confirmed a flown mission. The claim is a pitch-style summary and is broadly supported.
claims.summary: No NASA source confirms the hand actually flew on a space mission.

claims.text: Sergeant Garrett Anderson said he lost his arm in Iraq in 2005 from an improvised explosive device and that in his 18 years as an amputee, prosthetics he used were too heavy, too slow, not functional and not durable.
claims.argument: Several sources confirm that Sgt. Garrett Anderson, injured in Iraq in 2005, appeared in Psyonic's Shark Tank pitch (Season 15, 2024) and demonstrated the Ability Hand. None of the pages retrieved print his spoken lines, so the exact wording could not be checked against a transcript. The caption text is itself the speaker's own on-air statement, and it fits the confirmed facts of his injury.
claims.summary: Anderson did appear on Shark Tank for this hand, but his exact words were not found in text.

quote.author: Sergeant Garrett Anderson
quote.quoted_text: I lost my arm in Iraq in 2005 from an improvised explosive device. I've used a lot of prosthetics in my 18 years of being an amput. They're too heavy, too slow, not functional, and not durable.

claims.text: Dr. Adil Akar earned a bachelor's degree in biology from Loyola University Chicago, a master's in computer science, another master's in electrical and computer engineering, and a PhD in neuroscience, and left medical school.
claims.argument: The person is Aadeel Akhtar, founder of PSYONIC (maker of the Ability Hand); "Adil Akar" is a transcription error. Wikipedia and profiles say he earned a B.S. in Biology (2007) and an M.S. in Computer Science (2008) at Loyola University Chicago. He then earned an M.S. in Electrical & Computer Engineering and a PhD in Neuroscience at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Search summaries say he came to UIUC in 2010 for an MD/PhD program and left medical school to focus on the company. The wording "left medical school" is supported only by secondary sources, so confidence is somewhat reduced.
claims.summary: His degrees match; the name is Aadeel Akhtar, and he left an MD/PhD track.

claims.text: Psionic has raised $3.6 million so far.
claims.argument: BGR reports that PSYONIC (the bionic hand maker, spelled "Psionic" in the transcript) had raised $3.6 million, much of it from a StartEngine crowdfunding campaign, by its February 2024 Shark Tank appearance. This matches the speaker's figures: $3.6M total and about $2.2M from the crowdfunding campaign. A separate listing cites a campaign that had raised $2,229,648, and other sources report more than $10M in equity and grant funding by September 2025. The $3.6M figure therefore appears to come from the 2024 pitch, and it would be out of date as a 2026 total. The video was uploaded in June 2026, so the clip may be older footage.
claims.summary: The $3.6 million total is reported only for the 2024 pitch, not for 2026.

claims.text: Psionic raised $1.4 million at a $12 million valuation, and $2.2 million so far on StartEngine at a $50 million valuation, over almost a year.
claims.argument: Reports agree that PSYONIC's StartEngine crowdfunding was priced at about a $50 million valuation. Shark Tank Blog mentions $1.4 million at a $12 million valuation, but it pairs the $2.2 million with a $15 million valuation, which differs from the speaker's $50 million. Aggregators give conflicting totals ($3.1M, $3.87M, $6.9M), and the StartEngine page could not be read. The "almost a year" timing and the $2.2 million figure could not be checked against a filing, so the claim stays unconfirmed.
claims.summary: No source confirms the exact round sizes, though a $50 million StartEngine valuation is widely reported.

claims.text: Psionic has raised $2.4 million in grant funding and expects another $2.7 million next year from the DoD.
claims.argument: The founder's NSF SBIR grants list (225k + 225k + 937k + 1M) sums to about $2.39 million, matching the "$2.4 million in grant funding" figure; an Illinois article also cites about $2.4 million in NSF grants. A Defense Health Agency award of $2,635,000 (starting Sept 2025) is close to the "$2.7 million from the DoD" expected. Shark Tank coverage reports the same figures from the pitch. The DoD amount is roughly but not exactly matched, and no primary source states the "next year" expectation, so some doubt remains.
claims.summary: The $2.7 million expected next year from the DoD is not clearly confirmed by an official source.

claims.text: Half of Psionic's sales come from social media.
claims.argument: The company is spelled Psyonic. Blog recaps of its Shark Tank pitch say its founder told the panel that about half of its sales come through social media, and that this was why it used StartEngine. That matches what the speaker says. The only source is the company's own statement. No filing or audited data breaks down sales by channel. A University of Chicago Polsky Center item shows the company focused on social media marketing, which fits the claim but does not prove the 50% figure.
claims.summary: The company says half its sales come from social media, but no independent data confirms it.

claims.text: The Psionic ability hand is an FDA registered medical device and is covered by Medicare in the US.
claims.argument: An FDA registration listing shows PSYONIC's Ability Hand as a Class 1 device (product code IQZ), which fits "FDA registered". The company says it designed the hand to be Medicare-covered, and a supplier lists L6880 as its billing code. No Medicare PDAC verification record was found, so the coverage rests mainly on company statements. The FDA listing seen had an expiry of 2025, so it may be outdated.
claims.summary: No official Medicare verification record for this hand was found, only company statements.

claims.text: Before the ability hand came along, only 10% of patients in the US could afford a bionic hand.
claims.argument: Newsweek reports PSYONIC's CEO Akhtar saying only 10% of those who needed bionic limbs could previously afford them, and that Medicare coverage should raise access to about 75%. The speaker repeats this company figure faithfully. It is a company estimate, not measured data, and no independent study or survey of affordability was found. Medicare coverage of the Ability Hand is reported, which fits the context.
claims.summary: No independent source measures what share of US patients could afford a bionic hand.

claims.text: Psionic's hand costs $15,500.
claims.argument: Several secondary sources about Psyonic's Ability Hand, including Shark Tank coverage, give the price as $15,500 and the production cost as about $1,800. This matches the founder's statement in the video. One outlet's "$15,000" looks like a mix-up. The company name is spelled "Psyonic", but the product is the same.
claims.summary: The hand's price is reported as $15,500, matching what the founder says.

claims.text: It costs Psionic $1,800 to make one hand.
claims.argument: Coverage of the company (spelled Psyonic) and its Ability Hand, pitched on Shark Tank, repeats a $15,500 price and a $1,800 cost to make. A search summary of those outlets said Sportskeeda reported about $1,500 per unit and Marketrealist said $15,000, and it judged the $15,000 figure unreliable. The $1,800 figure is the founder's own statement, with no independent audit found, so some uncertainty remains. The spelling "Psionic" is just a variant of Psyonic.
claims.summary: The $1,800 build cost is the founder's own statement, and no outside audit of it was found.

claims.text: Psionic has over 100 patients.
claims.argument: The speaker's company appears to be PSYONIC (spelled "Psionic" in the claim). Its CEO has said in a San Diego Magazine piece that more than 250 people use its hand. That is consistent with "over 100 patients", though the article is undated and may be later than the pitch. Medicare coverage and the "10% could afford" figure also appear in the coverage found. No source gives the exact count at the time of the pitch.
claims.summary: No dated source gives the exact patient count at the time of the pitch.

claims.text: Psionic currently has a production capacity of about 100 hands a year.
claims.argument: The pitch comes from Psyonic's Shark Tank appearance (Season 15, aired early 2024), where the founder reportedly said he wanted to reach 500 units a year, which fits a lower current capacity. No retrieved source states a 100-per-year capacity directly. A later San Diego Magazine piece mentions current output of 1,000 hands a year, with an undated figure, so "currently" may be outdated by the 2026 upload. The claim is therefore plausible for 2024 but not verified, and not clearly right for 2026.
claims.summary: The 100-a-year figure matches the 2024 pitch, but no source confirms it or shows the 2026 capacity.

claims.text: Psionic is looking at potentially producing at least 500 hands per year by next year, and then a thousand and more.
claims.argument: No fact check available — this is a prediction about the future, which no source can confirm yet.

claims.text: Psionic needs up to $5 million in this round to reach a capacity of 1,000 units a year.
claims.argument: The claim is the founder's own estimate, given in the video. Searches found PSYONIC's Shark Tank deal ($1 million for 6%, meant to scale production) and an earlier crowdfunding round. They found no report of a round of up to $5 million, and none tying that sum to a 1,000-unit annual capacity. Secondary reports give conflicting production figures. Nothing contradicts the claim, but nothing confirms it either.
claims.summary: No source confirms the $5 million figure for reaching 1,000 units a year.

claims.text: Noah Galloway, a veteran and friend of the speaker from Dancing with the Stars, lost his arm and his leg.
claims.argument: Multiple outlets report that Army veteran Noah Galloway lost his left arm above the elbow and his left leg above the knee to a roadside bomb in Iraq in 2005. He competed on Dancing with the Stars season 20 in 2015 and finished third. The friendship with the speaker is personal and not checkable, but it is not contradicted.
claims.summary: Noah Galloway, an Iraq veteran, lost his left arm and left leg and danced on the show.

claims.text: Psionic's clinician or prosthetist makes the socket and then attaches Psionic's hand to it with all its electronics; Psionic makes just the hand.
claims.argument: PSYONIC (spelled "Psionic" in the video) sells the Ability Hand. Sources describe two parts: a socket that fits the residual limb, and the hand that attaches into the socket. The hand carries the electronics, with electrode sensors in the socket or a Bluetooth app for control. Clinicians handle fitting, and the company provides clinician setup guides. No source states outright that the company makes only the hand, but the description fits.
claims.summary: The company makes the hand; a clinician makes the socket and fits the hand into it.

claims.text: Psionic's lifetime sales are about $2 million.
claims.argument: Coverage of the Shark Tank Season 15 pitch (Feb 2024) says founder Dr. Aadeel Akhtar told the sharks lifetime sales were about $2 million. He also said sales were just over $1 million in the prior year, with about $100,000 profit. The company is spelled "Psyonic". The figure is the founder's on-air claim as of the 2024 filming, not an independently verified number, and one outlet notes the exact sales numbers are not public.
claims.summary: The founder said on the show that lifetime sales were about $2 million; that is his own figure.

claims.text: Psionic's sales last year were just over a million dollars.
claims.argument: The segment is from Shark Tank Season 15 (aired February 2024), where Psyonic's Dr. Aadeel Akhtar said lifetime sales were about $2 million and last year's were just over $1 million, with about $100,000 profit. Secondary coverage (Shark Tank Blog, Benzinga, BGR) reports about $1 million in sales for 2022, the year before the pitch. "Last year" means the year before the pitch, not the 2026 upload date. The figures are the founder's on-air claims and no audited numbers were found, but they match the claim.
claims.summary: The founder said on the show that last year's sales were just over $1 million, and coverage matches.

claims.text: Psionic made a profit of $100,000 on last year's sales.
claims.argument: Coverage of the Shark Tank pitch (Season 15, aired February 2024) says Psyonic founder Dr. Aadeel Akhtar told the sharks that lifetime sales were about $2 million. He said sales in the prior year (2022) were just over $1 million, with about $100,000 in profit. The "last year" in the claim is relative to the pitch, not to the 2026 upload date. The profit figure is the founder's own statement and is not independently audited. Psyonic's later sales and profit figures were not found.
claims.summary: On Shark Tank, the founder said sales were just over $1 million and profit was about $100,000.

claims.text: Psionic expects this year's sales to be at least around $2 million.
claims.argument: No fact check available — this is a prediction about the future, which no source can confirm yet.

claims.text: With preference shares, as more money is raised the holder's percentage is protected in perpetuity, so the holder is never diluted while all other shareholders are.
claims.argument: Standard preferred stock does not guarantee a fixed ownership percentage forever. Anti-dilution clauses adjust only for later sales at a lower price (down rounds), through weighted-average or full-ratchet conversion changes, and they are not in all preferred stock. Maintaining percentage in new rounds needs separate pre-emptive or pro-rata rights, which are usually limited to major investors and carve out things like option plans. A bespoke term guaranteeing a fixed percentage is possible if negotiated, but the general statement that preference shares make the holder never diluted is wrong.
claims.summary: Preferred shares don't automatically freeze your percentage; protection is limited and depends on the deal's terms.

claims.text: Psionic's founder says the company is going to be turned into a billion dollar company.
claims.argument: No fact check available — this is a prediction about the future, which no source can confirm yet.

claims.text: Kevin O'Leary offered $1 million for 10% of Psionic as standard common shares, with the option to invest more in the future, and said he would be diluted.
claims.argument: Coverage of the Season 15 Shark Tank pitch by Psyonic (the company's actual spelling) says Kevin O'Leary offered $1 million for 10% equity. This matches the transcript, where he calls them "standard common shares", asks for the option to invest more later, and says "I will be diluted". The sources do not quote the "option to invest more" wording, but they agree on the core offer. The deal later settled at 6% split among three sharks.
claims.summary: O'Leary did offer $1 million for 10% in plain common shares, saying he'd accept being diluted.

claims.text: Dr. Adil Akar's counter-offer was $1 million for 2% plus an extra 2% in advisory shares that are dilutive, i.e. $1 million for 4%.
claims.argument: The pitch was by Dr. Aadeel Akhtar of PSYONIC (Shark Tank Season 15), whose name is garbled in the claim. Sportskeeda describes a counter of $1 million for 2% plus 2% in advisory shares. Shark Tank Blog reports a counter of 2% plus 1% each in advisory shares, which is also 4% in total, and then a 4% non-dilutable counter. Sources differ slightly on the sequence of counters, but the $1 million for 4% summary matches the reporting and the speaker's own words.
claims.summary: The founder offered $1 million for 2% plus 2% in advisory shares, which adds up to 4%.

claims.text: Three Sharks (Kevin, Lori and Damon) agreed to invest together in Psionic, and the deal was settled at $1 million for 6% equity in common shares.
claims.argument: Reports on Psyonic's Shark Tank appearance (Season 15, aired Feb 2024) say Kevin O'Leary, Lori Greiner and Daymond John jointly offered $1 million for 6% equity, about 2% each. This matches the claim, since "Damon" is the transcript's spelling of Daymond and "Psionic" of Psyonic. One summary mentions common shares plus advisory shares, so the exact share structure is less certain, but the core deal terms are confirmed.
claims.summary: Kevin, Lori and Daymond together put in $1 million for 6% of Psyonic, as stated.

claims.text: According to Damon, Psionic's deal was seven and a half (as the speaker states it) with three sharks.
claims.argument: Articles on the Season 15 Psyonic pitch describe Daymond John, Lori Greiner and Kevin O'Leary teaming up for $1 million, with about 2% each (6% total) as the final terms. No retrieved page gives the negotiation transcript, so the "2 and 1/2 each, seven and a half" proposal could not be checked. "Damon" is most likely the captions' mis-hearing of Daymond.
claims.summary: The episode's deal is reported, but no record of this exact "seven and a half" wording was found.

quote.author: Damon
quote.quoted_text: So seven and a half according to Damon, three sharks.
